questions.question_text: The line $L_{1}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{a}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$ and the line $L_{2}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$ . The shortest distance between the lines $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is :
questions.question_html: The line $L_{1}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{a}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$ and the line $L_{2}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$ . The shortest distance between the lines $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: The line $L_{1}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{a}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$ . The line $L_{2}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$ . Equations of the Lines: Equation of $L_{1}$ : $r=7\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+2\hat{k}+\lambda(-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$ Equation of $L_{2}$ : $r=5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}+\mu(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ Shortest Distance Between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ : The formula for the shortest distance between two skew lines is given by: $\text{Distance}=|\frac{(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}|$ Calculations: Vector between the points: $\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}=(5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})-(7\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ Cross product of direction vectors: $\vec{b}_{1}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{b}_{2}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{aligned}|=2\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-7\hat{k}$ Magnitude of the cross product: $|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+17^{2}+(-7)^{2}}=\sqrt{342}$ Dot product: $(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})=(-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \cdot (2\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-7\hat{k})$ $=(-2)(2)+(-3)(17)+(2)(-7)=-4-51-14=-69$ Shortest Distance: $\text{Distance}=|\frac{-69}{\sqrt{342}}|=\frac{23}{\sqrt{38}}$
questions.explanation_html:
The line $L_{1}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{a}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$ . The line $L_{2}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$ .

Equations of the Lines:

Equation of $L_{1}$ :

$r=7\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+2\hat{k}+\lambda(-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$

Equation of $L_{2}$ :

$r=5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}+\mu(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$

Shortest Distance Between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ :

The formula for the shortest distance between two skew lines is given by:

$\text{Distance}=|\frac{(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}|$

Calculations:

Vector between the points:

$\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}=(5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})-(7\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

Cross product of direction vectors:

$\vec{b}_{1}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{b}_{2}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{aligned}|=2\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-7\hat{k}$

Magnitude of the cross product:

$|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+17^{2}+(-7)^{2}}=\sqrt{342}$

Dot product:

$(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})=(-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \cdot (2\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-7\hat{k})$

$=(-2)(2)+(-3)(17)+(2)(-7)=-4-51-14=-69$

Shortest Distance:

$\text{Distance}=|\frac{-69}{\sqrt{342}}|=\frac{23}{\sqrt{38}}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & L:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-2}{2}=\mu \\ & P(\mu+1,-\mu-1,2\mu+2) \\ & \vec{AP} \cdot \vec{d}=0 \Rightarrow (\mu,-\mu-3,2\mu) \cdot (1,-1,2)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \mu+\mu+3+4\mu=0 \Rightarrow \mu=-\frac{1}{2} \\ & \therefore P(\frac{-1}{2}+1,+\frac{1}{2}-1,2(\frac{-1}{2})+2) \\ & P(\frac{1}{2},\frac{-1}{2},1) \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \mu+1=-1+\lambda & -\mu-1=1-\lambda & 2\mu+2=-2+\lambda \\ \mu=\lambda-2 & \mu=\lambda-2 & ↓ \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & 2(\lambda-2)+2=-2+\lambda \\ & 2\lambda-4+2=-2+\lambda \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mu=-2,\lambda=0 \\ & \therefore Q \equiv (-1,1-2) \\ & P(\frac{1}{2},\frac{-1}{2},1)\text{and}Q(-1,1,-2) \\ & PQ=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{2}+1)^{2}+(\frac{-1}{2}-1)^{2}+(1+2)^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{9}{4}+9}=\sqrt{\frac{54}{4}} \\ & \therefore 2(PQ)^{2}=2(\frac{54}{4})=27 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & L:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-2}{2}=\mu \\ & P(\mu+1,-\mu-1,2\mu+2) \\ & \vec{AP} \cdot \vec{d}=0 \Rightarrow (\mu,-\mu-3,2\mu) \cdot (1,-1,2)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \mu+\mu+3+4\mu=0 \Rightarrow \mu=-\frac{1}{2} \\ & \therefore P(\frac{-1}{2}+1,+\frac{1}{2}-1,2(\frac{-1}{2})+2) \\ & P(\frac{1}{2},\frac{-1}{2},1) \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \mu+1=-1+\lambda & -\mu-1=1-\lambda & 2\mu+2=-2+\lambda \\ \mu=\lambda-2 & \mu=\lambda-2 & ↓ \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & 2(\lambda-2)+2=-2+\lambda \\ & 2\lambda-4+2=-2+\lambda \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mu=-2,\lambda=0 \\ & \therefore Q \equiv (-1,1-2) \\ & P(\frac{1}{2},\frac{-1}{2},1)\text{and}Q(-1,1,-2) \\ & PQ=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{2}+1)^{2}+(\frac{-1}{2}-1)^{2}+(1+2)^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{9}{4}+9}=\sqrt{\frac{54}{4}} \\ & \therefore 2(PQ)^{2}=2(\frac{54}{4})=27 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The distance of the line $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-6}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ from the point $(1,4,0)$ along the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+3}{3}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: To find the distance from the line $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-6}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ to the point $(1,4,0)$ along the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+3}{3},$ we first consider a parallel line passing through the point $(1,4,0)$ . The equation of this parallel line is: $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-4}{2}=\frac{z-0}{3}.$ Next, we find the point of intersection between the given line and the parallel line, which can be expressed in parameter form as: $(\lambda+1,2\lambda+4,3\lambda)=(2t+2,3t+6,4t+3).$ Solving for $\lambda$ in terms of $t$ , from the first coordinate: $\lambda=2t+1.$ Using the second coordinates, we equate: $2\lambda+4=3t+6 \Rightarrow 2(2t+1)+4=3t+6.$ Simplifying gives: $4t+2+4=3t+6 \Rightarrow 4t+6=3t+6 \Rightarrow t=0.$ Substituting $t=0$ into either line equation yields the point of intersection (POI) as: $(2,6,3).$ The distance from the point $(1,4,0)$ to the POI $(2,6,3)$ is computed as: $\sqrt{(2-1)^{2}+(6-4)^{2}+(3-0)^{2}}=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{14}.$
questions.explanation_html:
To find the distance from the line

$\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-6}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$

to the point $(1,4,0)$ along the line

$\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+3}{3},$

we first consider a parallel line passing through the point $(1,4,0)$ . The equation of this parallel line is:

$\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-4}{2}=\frac{z-0}{3}.$

Next, we find the point of intersection between the given line and the parallel line, which can be expressed in parameter form as:

$(\lambda+1,2\lambda+4,3\lambda)=(2t+2,3t+6,4t+3).$

Solving for $\lambda$ in terms of $t$ , from the first coordinate:

$\lambda=2t+1.$

Using the second coordinates, we equate:

$2\lambda+4=3t+6 \Rightarrow 2(2t+1)+4=3t+6.$

Simplifying gives:

$4t+2+4=3t+6 \Rightarrow 4t+6=3t+6 \Rightarrow t=0.$

Substituting $t=0$ into either line equation yields the point of intersection (POI) as:

$(2,6,3).$

The distance from the point $(1,4,0)$ to the POI $(2,6,3)$ is computed as:

$\sqrt{(2-1)^{2}+(6-4)^{2}+(3-0)^{2}}=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{14}.$

Dr's of $PQ<2\lambda-3\mu-1,3\lambda-4\mu-2$ ,

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{2\lambda-3\mu-1}{-1}=\frac{3\lambda-4\mu-2}{2}=\frac{4\lambda-5\mu-2}{-1} \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{3}\mu=\frac{-1}{6} \\ & \Rightarrow P(\frac{5}{3},3,\frac{13}{3})Q(\frac{3}{2},\frac{10}{3},\frac{25}{6}) \end{aligned}$

Dr's $PQ⟨1,-2,1⟩$

questions.question_html: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y+15}{-7}=\frac{z-9}{5}$ and $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-9}{-3}$ is
questions.explanation_text: Given two lines are represented as: $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y+15}{-7}=\frac{z-9}{5}$ and $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-9}{-3}$ The formula for the shortest distance between two lines is: $d=\frac{|(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})|}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}$ From the given lines: $\vec{a}_{1}=(3,-15,9)$ $\vec{a}_{2}=(-1,1,9)$ $\vec{b}_{1}=(2,-7,5)$ $\vec{b}_{2}=(2,1,-3)$ Calculate the difference: $\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}=(-1-3,1+15,9-9)=(-4,16,0)$ Next, compute the cross product: $\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{aligned}|=(16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k})$ The magnitude of the cross product is: $|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|=|(16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k})|=16\sqrt{3}$ Calculate the dot product: $(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})=(-4\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+0\hat{k}) \cdot (16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k})=-64+256+0=192$ Finally, find the shortest distance: $d=\frac{|192|}{16\sqrt{3}}=\frac{192}{16\sqrt{3}}=4\sqrt{3}$ Thus, the shortest distance is: $4\sqrt{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given two lines are represented as:

$\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y+15}{-7}=\frac{z-9}{5}$

and

$\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-9}{-3}$

The formula for the shortest distance between two lines is:

$d=\frac{|(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})|}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}$

From the given lines:

$\vec{a}_{1}=(3,-15,9)$

$\vec{a}_{2}=(-1,1,9)$

$\vec{b}_{1}=(2,-7,5)$

$\vec{b}_{2}=(2,1,-3)$

Calculate the difference:

$\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}=(-1-3,1+15,9-9)=(-4,16,0)$

Next, compute the cross product:

$\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{aligned}|=(16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k})$

The magnitude of the cross product is:

$|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|=|(16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k})|=16\sqrt{3}$

Calculate the dot product:

$(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})=(-4\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+0\hat{k}) \cdot (16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k})=-64+256+0=192$

Finally, find the shortest distance:

$d=\frac{|192|}{16\sqrt{3}}=\frac{192}{16\sqrt{3}}=4\sqrt{3}$

Thus, the shortest distance is:

$4\sqrt{3}$

questions.question_text: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ and $\frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is 1 , then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is :
questions.question_html:
If the shortest distance between the lines

$\frac{x-\lambda}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ and $\frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is 1 , then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Given the two lines: $L_{1}:\frac{x-\lambda}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ $L_{2}:\frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ We observe that these lines are not parallel as their directional vectors are not proportional. The directional vector for $L_{1}$ is $(-2,1,1)$ and for $L_{2}$ is $(1,-2,1)$ . The shortest distance between two skew (non-intersecting and non-parallel) lines in the three-dimensional space is along the line that is perpendicular to both lines. This implies we can find a vector that is perpendicular to both directional vectors by taking their cross product. The directional vector for $L_{1}$ is $d_{1}=⟨-2,1,1⟩$ , and for $L_{2}$ is $d_{2}=⟨1,-2,1⟩$ . The cross product of $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , which will be perpendicular to both lines, is given by: $d=d_{1} \times d_{2}=|\begin{aligned} i & j & k \\ -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ Expanding the determinate gives: $d=i((1)(1)-(1)(-2))-j((-2)(1)-(1)(1))+k((-2)(-2)-(1)(1))$ $d=i(1+2)-j(-2-1)+k(4-1)$ $d=3i+3j+3k$ $d=⟨3,3,3⟩$ The shortest distance $D$ between the two lines can then be given by the formula: $D=\frac{|(a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}) \cdot d|}{‖d‖}$ Where $a_{𝟏}$ and $a_{𝟐}$ are position vectors to any points on line $L_{1}$ and line $L_{2}$ , respectively, and ' $\cdot$ ' denotes the dot product. From the lines' equations, we can choose a point on each line (when the parameter is zero). Thus, for $L_{1}$ , let's choose the point $A(\lambda,2,1)$ , and for $L_{2}$ , let's choose the point $B(\sqrt{3},1,2)$ . These points correspond to the vectors $a_{𝟏}=⟨\lambda,2,1⟩$ and $a_{𝟐}=⟨\sqrt{3},1,2⟩$ , respectively. The vector $a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}$ is: $a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}=⟨\sqrt{3},1,2⟩-⟨\lambda,2,1⟩$ $a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}=⟨\sqrt{3}-\lambda,1-2,2-1⟩$ $a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}=⟨\sqrt{3}-\lambda,-1,1⟩$ We can now substitute this, along with $d$ , into the distance formula: $D=\frac{|(⟨\sqrt{3}-\lambda,-1,1⟩) \cdot ⟨3,3,3⟩|}{‖⟨3,3,3⟩‖}$ $D=\frac{|3(\sqrt{3}-\lambda)+3(-1)+3(1)|}{\sqrt{3^{2}+3^{2}+3^{2}}}$ $D=\frac{|3\sqrt{3}-3\lambda-3+3|}{\sqrt{27}}$ $D=\frac{|3\sqrt{3}-3\lambda|}{3\sqrt{3}}$ $D=\frac{|\sqrt{3}-\lambda|}{\sqrt{3}}$ Given that the shortest distance $D$ between the lines is 1, we can equate the above result to 1, and solve for $\lambda$ : $\frac{|\sqrt{3}-\lambda|}{\sqrt{3}}=1$ $|\sqrt{3}-\lambda|=\sqrt{3}$ This absolute value equation gives us two possible cases: Case 1: $\sqrt{3}-\lambda=\sqrt{3}$ , which gives $\lambda=0$ . Case 2: $\sqrt{3}-\lambda=-\sqrt{3}$ , which gives $\lambda=2\sqrt{3}$ . Therefore, the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is: $\lambda_{sum}=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=0+2\sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3}$ Hence, option B ( $2\sqrt{3}$ ) is the correct answer.
questions.explanation_html:
Given the two lines:

$L_{1}:\frac{x-\lambda}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$

$L_{2}:\frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$

We observe that these lines are not parallel as their directional vectors are not proportional. The directional vector for $L_{1}$ is $(-2,1,1)$ and for $L_{2}$ is $(1,-2,1)$ . The shortest distance between two skew (non-intersecting and non-parallel) lines in the three-dimensional space is along the line that is perpendicular to both lines. This implies we can find a vector that is perpendicular to both directional vectors by taking their cross product.

The directional vector for $L_{1}$ is $d_{1}=⟨-2,1,1⟩$ , and for $L_{2}$ is $d_{2}=⟨1,-2,1⟩$ . The cross product of $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , which will be perpendicular to both lines, is given by:

$d=d_{1} \times d_{2}=|\begin{aligned} i & j & k \\ -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{aligned}|$

Expanding the determinate gives:

$d=i((1)(1)-(1)(-2))-j((-2)(1)-(1)(1))+k((-2)(-2)-(1)(1))$

$d=i(1+2)-j(-2-1)+k(4-1)$

$d=3i+3j+3k$

$d=⟨3,3,3⟩$

The shortest distance $D$ between the two lines can then be given by the formula:

$D=\frac{|(a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}) \cdot d|}{‖d‖}$

Where $a_{𝟏}$ and $a_{𝟐}$ are position vectors to any points on line $L_{1}$ and line $L_{2}$ , respectively, and ' $\cdot$ ' denotes the dot product.

From the lines' equations, we can choose a point on each line (when the parameter is zero). Thus, for $L_{1}$ , let's choose the point $A(\lambda,2,1)$ , and for $L_{2}$ , let's choose the point $B(\sqrt{3},1,2)$ . These points correspond to the vectors $a_{𝟏}=⟨\lambda,2,1⟩$ and $a_{𝟐}=⟨\sqrt{3},1,2⟩$ , respectively.

The vector $a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}$ is:

$a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}=⟨\sqrt{3},1,2⟩-⟨\lambda,2,1⟩$

$a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}=⟨\sqrt{3}-\lambda,1-2,2-1⟩$

$a_{𝟐}-a_{𝟏}=⟨\sqrt{3}-\lambda,-1,1⟩$

We can now substitute this, along with $d$ , into the distance formula:

$D=\frac{|(⟨\sqrt{3}-\lambda,-1,1⟩) \cdot ⟨3,3,3⟩|}{‖⟨3,3,3⟩‖}$

$D=\frac{|3(\sqrt{3}-\lambda)+3(-1)+3(1)|}{\sqrt{3^{2}+3^{2}+3^{2}}}$

$D=\frac{|3\sqrt{3}-3\lambda-3+3|}{\sqrt{27}}$

$D=\frac{|3\sqrt{3}-3\lambda|}{3\sqrt{3}}$

$D=\frac{|\sqrt{3}-\lambda|}{\sqrt{3}}$

Given that the shortest distance $D$ between the lines is 1, we can equate the above result to 1, and solve for $\lambda$ :

$\frac{|\sqrt{3}-\lambda|}{\sqrt{3}}=1$

$|\sqrt{3}-\lambda|=\sqrt{3}$

This absolute value equation gives us two possible cases:

Case 1: $\sqrt{3}-\lambda=\sqrt{3}$ , which gives $\lambda=0$ .

Case 2: $\sqrt{3}-\lambda=-\sqrt{3}$ , which gives $\lambda=2\sqrt{3}$ .

Therefore, the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is:

$\lambda_{sum}=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=0+2\sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3}$

Hence, option B ( $2\sqrt{3}$ ) is the correct answer.

questions.explanation_text: $\text{Line}L \Rightarrow \frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y-3}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1}=\mu$ Point $M(\mu,\mu+3,-\mu+1)$ Direction vector of $QM=(\mu-3,\mu+6,-\mu)$ Direction vector of line $L=(1,1,-1)$ Both direction vector are perpendicular so $\begin{aligned} & 1 \times (\mu-3)+1 \times (\mu+6)-1 \times (-\mu)=0 \\ & \mu=-1 \end{aligned}$ Point $M(-1,2,2)$ midpoint of $PQ$ So point $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(-5,7,3)$ Area of $△PQR=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{PQ} \times \vec{QR}|$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{PQ}=(8,-10,-2) \\ & \vec{QR}=(-1,8,-2) \\ & \vec{PQ} \times \vec{QR}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 8 & -10 & -2 \\ -1 & 8 & -2 \end{aligned}|=36\hat{i}+18\hat{j}+54\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Area of $△PQR=\lambda$ $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(36)^{2}+(18)^{2}+(54)^{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \lambda^{2}=\frac{1}{4}(4536) \\ & \lambda^{2}=1134 \\ & \lambda^{2}=14K\text{(given)} \\ & 14K=1134 \\ & K=\frac{1134}{14}=81 \\ & K=81 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Given two lines: $\frac{x-x_{1}}{a_{1}}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{b_{1}}=\frac{z-z_{1}}{c_{1}}$ and $\frac{x-x_{2}}{a_{2}}=\frac{y-y_{2}}{b_{2}}=\frac{z-z_{2}}{c_{2}}$ These lines are coplanar if the determinant of the matrix $|\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|$ = 0 Now let's apply this condition to the given problem. The given line is : $\frac{x+3}{-3}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ So, the coordinates of any point on this line are $(-3,1,5)$ and the direction ratios are $(-3,1,5)$ . Now, let's calculate the determinants for each option and check which one equals zero. For Option A : $\frac{x+1}{-1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-5}{4}$ The coordinates of any point on this line are $(-1,2,5)$ and the direction ratios are $(-1,2,4)$ . The determinant is : $|\begin{aligned} -1-(-3) & 2-1 & 5-5 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 4 \end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 4 \end{aligned}|$ Applying the formula : = $2(1 \times 4-5 \times 2)-1((-3 \times 4)-(5 \times -1))+0((-3 \times 2)-(1 \times -1))$ = $2(4-10)-1(-12-(-5))+0(-6-(-1))$ = $2(-6)-1(-7)+0(-5)$ = $-12+7+0$ = $-5$ The determinant for Option A is not equal to zero, so this line is not coplanar with the given line. For Option B, we have : $\frac{x+1}{-1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ The coordinates of any point on this line are $(-1,2,5)$ and the direction ratios are $(-1,2,5)$ . $|\begin{aligned} -1-(-3) & 2-1 & 5-5 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{aligned}|$ Applying the formula, we get : = $2(1∗5-5∗2)-1((-3∗5)-(5∗-1))+0((-3∗2)-(1∗-1))$ = $2(5-10)-1(-15-(-5))+0(-6-(-1))$ = $2(-5)-1(-10)+0(-5)$ = $-10+10+0$ = $0$ So, the determinant for Option B equals zero, which confirms that the line in Option B is coplanar with the given line. For Option C : $\frac{x-1}{-1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ The coordinates of any point on this line are $(1,2,5)$ and the direction ratios are $(-1,2,5)$ . The determinant is: $|\begin{aligned} 1-(-3) & 2-1 & 5-5 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned} 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{aligned}|$ Applying the formula : = $4(1∗5-5∗2)-1((-3∗5)-(5∗-1))+0((-3∗2)-(1∗-1))$ = $4(5-10)-1(-15-(-5))+0(-6-(-1))$ = $4(-5)-1(-10)+0(-5)$ = $-20+10+0$ = $-10$ The determinant for Option C is not equal to zero, so this line is not coplanar with the given line. For Option D : $\frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ The coordinates of any point on this line are $(-1,2,5)$ and the direction ratios are $(1,2,5)$ . The determinant is : $|\begin{aligned} -1-(-3) & 2-1 & 5-5 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \end{aligned}|$ Applying the formula : = $2(1∗5-5∗2)-1((-3∗5)-(5∗1))+0((-3∗2)-(1∗1))$ = $2(5-10)-1(-15-5)+0(-6-1)$ = $2(-5)-1(-20)+0(-7)$ = $-10+20+0$ = $10$ So the determinant for Option D is not equal to zero, which means the line in Option D is not coplanar with the given line.

questions.explanation_text: We have, $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{6-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{5}$ intersect the line $\frac{x-5}{4}=\frac{y-7}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ and $\frac{x+3}{6}=\frac{3-y}{3}=\frac{z-6}{1}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\frac{x}{1}=\frac{6-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{5}=\lambda...........(i) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\lambda,y=6-2\lambda,z=5\lambda-8 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Also,}\frac{x-5}{4}=\frac{y-7}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}=k...........(ii) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=4k+5,y=3k+7,z=k-2 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+3}{6}=\frac{3-y}{3}=\frac{z-6}{1}=\mu..........(iii) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=6\mu-3,y=3-3\mu,z=\mu+6 \end{aligned}$ On solving Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\lambda=1,k=-1$ $\therefore$ Co-ordinate of $A$ is $(1,4,-3)$ On solving Eqs. (i) and (iii), we get $\lambda=3,\mu=1$ $\therefore$ Co-ordinate of $\beta$ is $(3,0,7)$ Co-ordinate of mid-point of $AB$ is $(\frac{1+3}{2},\frac{4+0}{2},\frac{-3+7}{2})$ or $(2,2,2)$ Perpendicular distance of mid-point of $AB$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=14$ is $\frac{|2(2)-2(2)+2-14|}{\sqrt{2^{2}+(-2)^{2}+1^{2}}}=4$
questions.explanation_html:
We have, $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{6-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{5}$ intersect the line

$\frac{x-5}{4}=\frac{y-7}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ and $\frac{x+3}{6}=\frac{3-y}{3}=\frac{z-6}{1}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\frac{x}{1}=\frac{6-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{5}=\lambda...........(i) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\lambda,y=6-2\lambda,z=5\lambda-8 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Also,}\frac{x-5}{4}=\frac{y-7}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}=k...........(ii) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=4k+5,y=3k+7,z=k-2 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+3}{6}=\frac{3-y}{3}=\frac{z-6}{1}=\mu..........(iii) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=6\mu-3,y=3-3\mu,z=\mu+6 \end{aligned}$

On solving Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\lambda=1,k=-1$

$\therefore$ Co-ordinate of $A$ is $(1,4,-3)$

On solving Eqs. (i) and (iii), we get $\lambda=3,\mu=1$

$\therefore$ Co-ordinate of $\beta$ is $(3,0,7)$

Co-ordinate of mid-point of $AB$ is $(\frac{1+3}{2},\frac{4+0}{2},\frac{-3+7}{2})$ or $(2,2,2)$

Perpendicular distance of mid-point of $AB$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=14$ is

$\frac{|2(2)-2(2)+2-14|}{\sqrt{2^{2}+(-2)^{2}+1^{2}}}=4$

questions.explanation_text: Given plane $\vec{r} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=6$ and $\vec{r} \cdot (2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})=-5$ Equation of plane passing through both plane $\begin{aligned} & P_{1} \rightarrow (x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+2\hat{k})(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=6 \\ \\ & P_{1}=x+y+z=6 \\ \\ & P_{2} \rightarrow (x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}) \cdot (2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})=-5 \\ \\ & P_{2} \rightarrow =2x+3y+4z=-5 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & P_{1}+\lambda P_{2}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (x+y+z-6)+\lambda(2x+3y+4z+5)=0 \end{aligned}$ passes through $(0,2,-2)$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (0+2-2-6)+\lambda(2 \times 0+3 \times 2+4 \times (-2)+5)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=2 \end{aligned}$ Equation of plane $5x+7y+9z+4=0$ $\therefore$ Distance of the point $(12,12,18)$ from the plane $\begin{aligned} d & =\frac{5 \times 12+7 \times 12+9 \times 18+4}{\sqrt{5^{2}+7^{2}+9^{2}}} \\ \\ & =\frac{60+84+162+4}{\sqrt{155}}=\frac{310}{\sqrt{155}} \\ \\ \therefore d^{2} & =\frac{310 \times 310}{155}=620 \end{aligned}$

passes through $(0,2,-2)$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (0+2-2-6)+\lambda(2 \times 0+3 \times 2+4 \times (-2)+5)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=2 \end{aligned}$

Equation of plane

$5x+7y+9z+4=0$

$\therefore$ Distance of the point $(12,12,18)$ from the plane

$\begin{aligned} d & =\frac{5 \times 12+7 \times 12+9 \times 18+4}{\sqrt{5^{2}+7^{2}+9^{2}}} \\ \\ & =\frac{60+84+162+4}{\sqrt{155}}=\frac{310}{\sqrt{155}} \\ \\ \therefore d^{2} & =\frac{310 \times 310}{155}=620 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: $l=\frac{1}{2},m=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},n=cos\theta$ $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}+n^{2}=1 \Rightarrow n^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow n=+\frac{1}{2}$ $\theta$ is acute $\therefore$ $n=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{v}=k(\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{k}),k \in R$ $\vec{v}.(\vec{a}-\vec{b})=0$ $(\sqrt{2}-a)\frac{1}{2}+(-1-b)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+(1-c)\frac{1}{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{a}{2}+\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{c}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow a+\sqrt{2}b+c=1$
questions.explanation_html:
$l=\frac{1}{2},m=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},n=cos\theta$

$l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}+n^{2}=1 \Rightarrow n^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow n=+\frac{1}{2}$

$\theta$ is acute $\therefore$ $n=\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{v}=k(\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{k}),k \in R$

$\vec{v}.(\vec{a}-\vec{b})=0$

$(\sqrt{2}-a)\frac{1}{2}+(-1-b)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+(1-c)\frac{1}{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{a}{2}+\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{c}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow a+\sqrt{2}b+c=1$

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+3}{1}=\lambda$ (say) & $\frac{x-a}{2}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\mu$ (say) $\therefore$ $\lambda+1=2\mu+a$ ...... (i) $2\lambda+2=3\mu-2$ ..... (ii) $\lambda-3=\mu+3$ .... (iii) By (i) & (ii) $\Rightarrow 3\mu-2=4\mu+2a+2$ $\mu=-2(1+a)$ & $\lambda=5-3a$ Put $\lambda$ & $\mu$ in (iii) we get $a=-9$ $\mu=16$ $\lambda=22$ $\therefore$ Point of intersection $\equiv (23,46,19)$ Distance from $z=-9$ is 28

& $\frac{x-a}{2}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\mu$ (say)

$\therefore$ $\lambda+1=2\mu+a$ ...... (i)

$\lambda-3=\mu+3$ .... (iii)

By (i) & (ii)

questions.question_text: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,3)$ in the plane $2x-y+z=9$ be $Q$ . If the coordinates of the point $R$ are $(6,10,7)$ , then the square of the area of the triangle $PQR$ is _____________.
questions.question_html: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,3)$ in the plane $2x-y+z=9$ be $Q$ . If the coordinates of the point $R$ are $(6,10,7)$ , then the square of the area of the triangle $PQR$ is _____________.
questions.explanation_text: Let $Q(x,y,z)$ be the image of $P(1,2,3)$ in the plane $\begin{aligned} & 2x-y+z=9 \\ \\ & \therefore \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\frac{-2(2 \times 1+(-1)(2)+(1)(3)(-9)}{(2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\frac{-2(-6)}{6}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=5,y=0,z=5 \end{aligned}$ Now, $\vec{PQ}=4\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{PR}=5\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ Area of the $△PQR=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{PQ} \times \vec{PR}|$ Now, $\vec{PQ} \times \vec{PR}$ $\begin{aligned} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & 8 & 4 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\hat{i}(-8-16)-\hat{j}(16-10)+\hat{k}(32+10) \\ \\ & =-24\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+42\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \therefore \frac{1}{2}|(-24\hat{i} & -6\hat{j}+42\hat{k})|=|-12\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+21\hat{k}| \\ \\ & =\sqrt{(-12)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(21)^{2}} \\ \\ & =\sqrt{144+9+441}=\sqrt{594} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ The square of the area of the $△PQR=594$

questions.question_text: Let the equation of the plane P containing the line $x+10=\frac{8-y}{2}=z$ be $ax+by+3z=2(a+b)$ and the distance of the plane $P$ from the point (1, 27, 7) be $c$ . Then $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: Let the equation of the plane P containing the line $x+10=\frac{8-y}{2}=z$ be $ax+by+3z=2(a+b)$ and the distance of the plane $P$ from the point (1, 27, 7) be $c$ . Then $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: The line $\frac{x+10}{1}=\frac{y-8}{-2}=\frac{z}{1}$ have a point $(-10,8,0)$ with d. r. $(1,-2,1)$ $\because$ the plane $ax+by+3z=2(a+b)$ $\Rightarrow b=2a$ $&$ dot product of d.r.'s is zero $\therefore a-2b+3=0$ $\therefore a=1&b=2$ Distance from $(1,27,7)$ is $c=\frac{1+54+21-6}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{70}{\sqrt{14}}=5\sqrt{14}$ $\therefore a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=1+4+350$ $=355$

$\Rightarrow b=2a$

$&$ dot product of d.r.'s is zero

$\therefore a-2b+3=0$ $\therefore a=1&b=2$

Distance from $(1,27,7)$ is

$c=\frac{1+54+21-6}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{70}{\sqrt{14}}=5\sqrt{14}$

$\therefore a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=1+4+350$

$=355$

questions.question_text: If the shortest between the lines $\frac{x+\sqrt{6}}{2}=\frac{y-\sqrt{6}}{3}=\frac{z-\sqrt{6}}{4}$ and $\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2\sqrt{6}}{4}=\frac{z+2\sqrt{6}}{5}$ is 6, then the square of sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is :
questions.question_html: If the shortest between the lines $\frac{x+\sqrt{6}}{2}=\frac{y-\sqrt{6}}{3}=\frac{z-\sqrt{6}}{4}$ and $\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2\sqrt{6}}{4}=\frac{z+2\sqrt{6}}{5}$ is 6, then the square of sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+\sqrt{6}}{2}=\frac{y-\sqrt{6}}{3}=\frac{z-\sqrt{6}}{4}$ $\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2\sqrt{6}}{4}=\frac{2+2\sqrt{6}}{5}$ is 6 Vector along line of shortest distance $=|\begin{aligned} i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \end{aligned}|, \Rightarrow -\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-k$ (its magnitude is $\sqrt{6}$ ) Now $\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}|\begin{aligned} \sqrt{6}+\lambda & \sqrt{6} & -3\sqrt{6} \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \end{aligned}|= \pm 6$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=-2\sqrt{6},10\sqrt{6}$ So, square of sum of these values $=(10\sqrt{6}-2\sqrt{6})^{2}=(8\sqrt{6})^{2}=384$
questions.explanation_html:
Shortest distance between the lines

$\frac{x+\sqrt{6}}{2}=\frac{y-\sqrt{6}}{3}=\frac{z-\sqrt{6}}{4}$

$\frac{x-\lambda}{3}=\frac{y-2\sqrt{6}}{4}=\frac{2+2\sqrt{6}}{5}$ is 6

Vector along line of shortest distance

$=|\begin{aligned} i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \end{aligned}|, \Rightarrow -\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-k$ (its magnitude is $\sqrt{6}$ )

Now $\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}|\begin{aligned} \sqrt{6}+\lambda & \sqrt{6} & -3\sqrt{6} \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \end{aligned}|= \pm 6$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=-2\sqrt{6},10\sqrt{6}$

So, square of sum of these values

$=(10\sqrt{6}-2\sqrt{6})^{2}=(8\sqrt{6})^{2}=384$

questions.question_text: Let the foot of perpendicular of the point $P(3,-2,-9)$ on the plane passing through the points $(-1,-2,-3),(9,3,4),(9,-2,1)$ be $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ . Then the distance of $Q$ from the origin is :
questions.question_html: Let the foot of perpendicular of the point $P(3,-2,-9)$ on the plane passing through the points $(-1,-2,-3),(9,3,4),(9,-2,1)$ be $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ . Then the distance of $Q$ from the origin is :
questions.explanation_text: The equation of the plane passing through points $A(-1,-2,-3)$ , $B(9,3,4)$ , and $C(9,-2,1)$ can be written using the determinant : $|\begin{aligned} x+1 & y+2 & z+3 \\ 10 & 5 & 7 \\ 10 & 0 & 4 \end{aligned}|=0$ Expanding the determinant, we get : $2x+3y-5z-7=0$ Next, we find the foot of the perpendicular from point $P(3,-2,-9)$ to the plane. Using the coordinates of $P$ and the equation of the plane, we can find the ratio of the perpendicular distance to the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$ , $y$ , and $z$ : $\frac{2(3)+3(-2)-5(-9)-7}{2^{2}+3^{2}+(-5)^{2}}=\frac{-38}{38}$ We can now find the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular, $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ : $\frac{\alpha-3}{2}=\frac{\beta+2}{3}=\frac{\gamma+9}{-5}=-\frac{38}{38}$ Solving for $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , and $\gamma$ : $\alpha=3-2(-\frac{38}{38})=1$ $\beta=-2+3(-\frac{38}{38})=-5$ $\gamma=-9-5(-\frac{38}{38})=-4$ So, the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular are $Q(1,-5,-4)$ . Now, we can find the distance of point $Q$ from the origin : $OQ=\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}}=\sqrt{1^{2}+(-5)^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=\sqrt{42}$
questions.explanation_html:
The equation of the plane passing through points $A(-1,-2,-3)$ , $B(9,3,4)$ , and $C(9,-2,1)$ can be written using the determinant :

$|\begin{aligned} x+1 & y+2 & z+3 \\ 10 & 5 & 7 \\ 10 & 0 & 4 \end{aligned}|=0$

Expanding the determinant, we get :

$2x+3y-5z-7=0$

Next, we find the foot of the perpendicular from point $P(3,-2,-9)$ to the plane. Using the coordinates of $P$ and the equation of the plane, we can find the ratio of the perpendicular distance to the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$ , $y$ , and $z$ :

$\frac{2(3)+3(-2)-5(-9)-7}{2^{2}+3^{2}+(-5)^{2}}=\frac{-38}{38}$

We can now find the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular, $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ :

$\frac{\alpha-3}{2}=\frac{\beta+2}{3}=\frac{\gamma+9}{-5}=-\frac{38}{38}$

Solving for $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , and $\gamma$ :

$\alpha=3-2(-\frac{38}{38})=1$

$\beta=-2+3(-\frac{38}{38})=-5$

$\gamma=-9-5(-\frac{38}{38})=-4$

So, the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular are $Q(1,-5,-4)$ . Now, we can find the distance of point $Q$ from the origin :

$OQ=\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}}=\sqrt{1^{2}+(-5)^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=\sqrt{42}$

questions.question_html: The plane, passing through the points $(0,-1,2)$ and $(-1,2,1)$ and parallel to the line passing through $(5,1,-7)$ and $(1,-1,-1)$ , also passes through the point :
questions.explanation_text: The first step is to find the normal vector to the desired plane. Since the plane is parallel to the line passing through the points (5, 1, -7) and (1, -1, -1), the direction vector of that line is also parallel to the plane. The direction vector is the difference between the coordinates of the two points, which is (5-1, 1-(-1), -7-(-1)) = (4, 2, -6). Next, let's find another vector that is parallel to the plane. This vector can be obtained by taking the difference between the coordinates of the points (0, -1, 2) and (-1, 2, 1), which the plane passes through. This gives us a vector of (0-(-1), -1-2, 2-1) = (1, -3, 1). The normal to the plane is perpendicular to both these vectors. It can be found by taking the cross product of the two vectors. The cross product of vectors (4, 2, -6) and (1, -3, 1) is : $\begin{aligned} & \vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 2 & -6 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}(-16)-\hat{j}(+10)+\hat{k}(-14) \\ \\ & =-16\hat{i}-10\hat{j}-14\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ The equation of the plane can now be written in the form : -16x - 10y - 14z = d We can find the constant 'd' by substituting one of the points through which the plane passes, say (0, -1, 2) : d = -16.0 -10.(-1) -14.2 = 10 - 28 = -18 So, the equation of the plane is -16x - 10y - 14z = -18. Now, we substitute the given options into the equation to check which one satisfies it : Option A: (-16.0 -10.5 -14.(-2) = -18) => -50 + 28 = -22 ≠ -18, so A is not correct. Option B: (-16.2 -10.0 -14.1 = -18) => -32 - 14 = -46 ≠ -18, so B is not correct. Option C: (-16.1 -10.(-2) -14.1 = -18) => -16 + 20 -14 = -10 ≠ -18, so C is not correct. Option D: (-16.(-2) -10.5 -14.0 = -18) => 32 - 50 = -18, so D is correct. So, the plane also passes through the point given in Option D, which is (-2, 5, 0).
questions.explanation_html:
The first step is to find the normal vector to the desired plane. Since the plane is parallel to the line passing through the points (5, 1, -7) and (1, -1, -1), the direction vector of that line is also parallel to the plane. The direction vector is the difference between the coordinates of the two points, which is (5-1, 1-(-1), -7-(-1)) = (4, 2, -6).

Next, let's find another vector that is parallel to the plane. This vector can be obtained by taking the difference between the coordinates of the points (0, -1, 2) and (-1, 2, 1), which the plane passes through. This gives us a vector of (0-(-1), -1-2, 2-1) = (1, -3, 1).

The normal to the plane is perpendicular to both these vectors. It can be found by taking the cross product of the two vectors.

The cross product of vectors (4, 2, -6) and (1, -3, 1) is :

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 2 & -6 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}(-16)-\hat{j}(+10)+\hat{k}(-14) \\ \\ & =-16\hat{i}-10\hat{j}-14\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

The equation of the plane can now be written in the form :

-16x - 10y - 14z = d

We can find the constant 'd' by substituting one of the points through which the plane passes, say (0, -1, 2) :

d = -16.0 -10.(-1) -14.2 = 10 - 28 = -18

So, the equation of the plane is -16x - 10y - 14z = -18.

Now, we substitute the given options into the equation to check which one satisfies it :

Option A: (-16.0 -10.5 -14.(-2) = -18) => -50 + 28 = -22 ≠ -18, so A is not correct.

Option B: (-16.2 -10.0 -14.1 = -18) => -32 - 14 = -46 ≠ -18, so B is not correct.

Option C: (-16.1 -10.(-2) -14.1 = -18) => -16 + 20 -14 = -10 ≠ -18, so C is not correct.

Option D: (-16.(-2) -10.5 -14.0 = -18) => 32 - 50 = -18, so D is correct.

So, the plane also passes through the point given in Option D, which is (-2, 5, 0).

questions.explanation_text: Co-ordinate of image of point $P(2,3,5)$ in the plane $2x+y-3z=6$ is $\begin{aligned} \frac{\alpha-2}{2} & =\frac{\beta-3}{1}=\frac{\gamma-5}{-3}=\frac{-2(2 \times 2+3-3 \times 5-6)}{2^{2}+1^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\ \\ \frac{\alpha-2}{2} & =\frac{\beta-3}{1}=\frac{\gamma-5}{-3}=2 \\ \\ \frac{\alpha-2}{2} & =2,\frac{\beta-3}{1}=2,\frac{\gamma-5}{-3}=2 \\ \\ \alpha & =6,\beta=5,\gamma=-1 \end{aligned}$ Hence, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=6+5-1=10$
questions.explanation_html:
Co-ordinate of image of point $P(2,3,5)$ in the plane $2x+y-3z=6$ is

Hence, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=6+5-1=10$

questions.question_text: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+2}{1}=\frac{y}{-2}=\frac{z-5}{2}$ and $\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+3}{0}$ is :
questions.question_html: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+2}{1}=\frac{y}{-2}=\frac{z-5}{2}$ and $\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+3}{0}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, the lines are $\begin{aligned} \frac{x+2}{1} & =\frac{y}{-2}=\frac{z-5}{2}..........(i) \\ \\ \text{and}\frac{x-4}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+3}{0}..........(ii) \end{aligned}$ Formula for shortest distance between two skew-lines, $\begin{aligned} SD & =|\frac{|\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|}|=|\frac{|\begin{aligned} 6 & 1 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{aligned}|}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{6(-4)-1(-2)-8(4)}{|-4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}|}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{-24+2-32}{\sqrt{36}}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{-54}{6}|=|-9|=9 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:

Formula for shortest distance between two skew-lines,

$\begin{aligned} SD & =|\frac{|\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|}|=|\frac{|\begin{aligned} 6 & 1 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{aligned}|}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{6(-4)-1(-2)-8(4)}{|-4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}|}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{-24+2-32}{\sqrt{36}}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{-54}{6}|=|-9|=9 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $P$ be the plane passing through the line $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-3}=\frac{z+5}{7}$ and the point $(2,4,-3)$ . If the image of the point $(-1,3,4)$ in the plane P is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $P$ be the plane passing through the line

$\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-3}=\frac{z+5}{7}$ and the point $(2,4,-3)$ .

If the image of the point $(-1,3,4)$ in the plane P

is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of line : $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-3}=\frac{z+5}{7}$ Let $B \equiv (2,4,-3)$ So, $\vec{AB}=(2-1)\hat{i}+(4-2)\hat{j}+(-3+5)\hat{k}$ $=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -3 & 7 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \end{aligned}|=(-6-14)\hat{i}-(2-7)\hat{j}+(2+3)\hat{k} \\ \\ & =-20\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+5\hat{k} \\ \\ & =-5(4\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Equation of plane is : $4(x-1)+(-1)(y-2)-1(z+5)=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 4x-4-y+2-z-5=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4x-y-z-7=0 \end{aligned}$ $\because$ Image of point $(-1,3,4)$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\frac{\alpha+1}{4}=\frac{\beta-3}{-1}=\frac{\gamma-4}{-1}=\frac{-2(-4-3-4-7)}{16+1+1}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=7,\beta=1,\gamma=2 \\ \\ & \text{So,}\alpha+\beta+\gamma=10 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of line : $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-3}=\frac{z+5}{7}$

Let $B \equiv (2,4,-3)$


So, $\vec{AB}=(2-1)\hat{i}+(4-2)\hat{j}+(-3+5)\hat{k}$

$=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -3 & 7 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \end{aligned}|=(-6-14)\hat{i}-(2-7)\hat{j}+(2+3)\hat{k} \\ \\ & =-20\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+5\hat{k} \\ \\ & =-5(4\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Equation of plane is :

$4(x-1)+(-1)(y-2)-1(z+5)=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 4x-4-y+2-z-5=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4x-y-z-7=0 \end{aligned}$

$\because$ Image of point $(-1,3,4)$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\frac{\alpha+1}{4}=\frac{\beta-3}{-1}=\frac{\gamma-4}{-1}=\frac{-2(-4-3-4-7)}{16+1+1}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=7,\beta=1,\gamma=2 \\ \\ & \text{So,}\alpha+\beta+\gamma=10 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let the line $L$ pass through the point $(0,1,2)$ , intersect the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ and be parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$ . Then the distance of the point $P(1,-9,2)$ from the line $L$ is :
questions.question_html: Let the line $L$ pass through the point $(0,1,2)$ , intersect the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ and be parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$ . Then the distance of the point $P(1,-9,2)$ from the line $L$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Given line, $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\lambda$ .........(i) $\therefore$ Any point on the line $A(2\lambda+1,3\lambda+2,\lambda+3)$ Since, line $L$ pass through the point $B(0,1,2)$ and intersects line (i) $\therefore$ Direction ratio of $AB$ are $\begin{aligned} & 0-2\lambda-1,1-3\lambda-2,2-\lambda-3 \\ \\ & \text{i.e.,}-2\lambda-1,-3\lambda-1,-\lambda-1 \end{aligned}$ Line $L$ parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 2(-2\lambda-1)+1(-3\lambda-1)-3(-\lambda-1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4\lambda-2-3\lambda-1+3\lambda+3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=0 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Direction ratio of}AB=-1,-1,-1 \\ \\ & \text{i.e.,}1,1,1 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Equation of line $L$ is $\frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-2}{1}=\mu$ $\Rightarrow x=\mu,y=\mu+1,z=\mu+2$ $\therefore$ Direction ratios of $PQ=\mu-1,\mu+10,\mu$ Since, $PQ⟂L$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 1(\mu-1)+1(\mu+10)+\mu(1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \mu-1+\mu+10+\mu=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 3\mu+9=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \mu=-3 \\ \\ & \therefore Q\text{is}(-3,-2,-1) \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Distance of the point $P(1,-9,2)$ from the line $L$ is $\begin{aligned} =\sqrt{(-3-1)^{2}+(-2+9)^{2}+(-1-2)^{2}} \\ \\ =\sqrt{16+49+9}=\sqrt{74} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given line, $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\lambda$ .........(i)

$\therefore$ Any point on the line $A(2\lambda+1,3\lambda+2,\lambda+3)$

Since, line $L$ pass through the point $B(0,1,2)$ and intersects line (i)

$\therefore$ Direction ratio of $AB$ are

$\begin{aligned} & 0-2\lambda-1,1-3\lambda-2,2-\lambda-3 \\ \\ & \text{i.e.,}-2\lambda-1,-3\lambda-1,-\lambda-1 \end{aligned}$

Line $L$ parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore 2(-2\lambda-1)+1(-3\lambda-1)-3(-\lambda-1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4\lambda-2-3\lambda-1+3\lambda+3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=0 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Direction ratio of}AB=-1,-1,-1 \\ \\ & \text{i.e.,}1,1,1 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Equation of line $L$ is $\frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-2}{1}=\mu$

$\Rightarrow x=\mu,y=\mu+1,z=\mu+2$



$\therefore$ Direction ratios of $PQ=\mu-1,\mu+10,\mu$

Since, $PQ⟂L$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore 1(\mu-1)+1(\mu+10)+\mu(1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \mu-1+\mu+10+\mu=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 3\mu+9=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \mu=-3 \\ \\ & \therefore Q\text{is}(-3,-2,-1) \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Distance of the point $P(1,-9,2)$ from the line $L$ is

$\begin{aligned} =\sqrt{(-3-1)^{2}+(-2+9)^{2}+(-1-2)^{2}} \\ \\ =\sqrt{16+49+9}=\sqrt{74} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html:
The shortest distance between the lines

$\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-4}{-3}$ and

$\frac{x+3}{1}=\frac{y+5}{4}=\frac{z-1}{-5}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & L_{1}:\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-4}{-3} \\ \\ & \vec{a_{1}}=5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{r_{1}}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \\ \\ & L_{2}:\frac{x+3}{1}=\frac{y+5}{4}=\frac{z-1}{-5} \\ \\ & \vec{a_{2}}=-3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{r_{2}}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-5\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 4 & -5 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Shortest distance (d)}=|\frac{(\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}) \cdot (\vec{a_{1}}-\vec{a_{2}})}{|\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}|}| \\ \\ & =\frac{36}{2\sqrt{3}}=6\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & L_{1}:\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-4}{-3} \\ \\ & \vec{a_{1}}=5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{r_{1}}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \\ \\ & L_{2}:\frac{x+3}{1}=\frac{y+5}{4}=\frac{z-1}{-5} \\ \\ & \vec{a_{2}}=-3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{r_{2}}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-5\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 4 & -5 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Shortest distance (d)}=|\frac{(\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}) \cdot (\vec{a_{1}}-\vec{a_{2}})}{|\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}|}| \\ \\ & =\frac{36}{2\sqrt{3}}=6\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If a plane passes through the points $(-1,k,0),(2,k,-1),(1,1,2)$ and is parallel to the line $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{2y+1}{2}=\frac{z+1}{-1}$ , then the value of $\frac{k^{2}+1}{(k-1)(k-2)}$ is :
questions.question_html: If a plane passes through the points $(-1,k,0),(2,k,-1),(1,1,2)$ and is parallel to the line $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{2y+1}{2}=\frac{z+1}{-1}$ , then the value of $\frac{k^{2}+1}{(k-1)(k-2)}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $P \equiv (-1,k,0),Q \equiv (2,k,-1)$ & $R(1,1,2)$ $\vec{P}R=2\hat{i}+(1-k)\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ & $\vec{Q}R=-\hat{i}+(1-k)\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ Normal to plane will be $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & (1-k) & 2 \\ -1 & (1-k) & 3 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}(1-k)-\hat{j}(8)+3\hat{k}(1-k)$ If line is parallel to this we have $1(1-k)+1(-8)+(-3)(1-k)=0$ $\Rightarrow 2(1-k)=-8$ $\Rightarrow 1-k=-4 \Rightarrow k=5$ $\therefore$ $\frac{k^{2}+1}{(k-1)(k-2)}=\frac{26}{4.3}=\frac{13}{6}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $P \equiv (-1,k,0),Q \equiv (2,k,-1)$ & $R(1,1,2)$

$\vec{P}R=2\hat{i}+(1-k)\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

& $\vec{Q}R=-\hat{i}+(1-k)\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ Normal to plane will be

$|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & (1-k) & 2 \\ -1 & (1-k) & 3 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}(1-k)-\hat{j}(8)+3\hat{k}(1-k)$

If line is parallel to this we have

$1(1-k)+1(-8)+(-3)(1-k)=0$

$\Rightarrow 2(1-k)=-8$

$\Rightarrow 1-k=-4 \Rightarrow k=5$

$\therefore$ $\frac{k^{2}+1}{(k-1)(k-2)}=\frac{26}{4.3}=\frac{13}{6}$

questions.question_html: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+8}{-7}=\frac{z-4}{5}$ and $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-6}{-3}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{r}_{1}=\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ $\vec{r}_{2}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}-7\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ S.D. $=\frac{|\begin{aligned} \vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2} & \begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}|}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$ $[\begin{aligned} \vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2} & \begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}]=|\begin{aligned} 0 & -10 & -2 \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{aligned}|$ $\therefore$ $10(-16)-2(16)=-192$ $|[\begin{aligned} \vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2} & \begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}]|=192$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{aligned}|=16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k}$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=16\sqrt{3}$ S.D. $=\frac{192}{16\sqrt{3}}=4\sqrt{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{r}_{1}=\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$

$\vec{r}_{2}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$

$\vec{a}=2\hat{i}-7\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$

S.D. $=\frac{|\begin{aligned} \vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2} & \begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}|}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$

$[\begin{aligned} \vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2} & \begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}]=|\begin{aligned} 0 & -10 & -2 \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{aligned}|$

$\therefore$ $10(-16)-2(16)=-192$

$|[\begin{aligned} \vec{r}_{1}-\vec{r}_{2} & \begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}]|=192$

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -7 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{aligned}|=16\hat{i}+16\hat{j}+16\hat{k}$

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=16\sqrt{3}$

S.D. $=\frac{192}{16\sqrt{3}}=4\sqrt{3}$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $\frac{x+4}{3}=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-3}{12}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{x+4}{3}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-3}{12}$ Equation of line passing through the point P $(-1,9,-16)$ and parallel to line $\frac{x+4}{3}=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-3}{12}$ is $\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{y-9}{-4}=\frac{z+16}{12}=\lambda$ Any point on this line (A) $=(3\lambda-1,-4\lambda+9,12\lambda-16)$ Point of intersection line and plane $\begin{aligned} & 2(3\lambda-1)+3(-4\lambda+9)-1(12\lambda-16)=5 \\ \\ \Rightarrow & 6\lambda-2-12\lambda+27-12\lambda+16=5 \\ \\ \Rightarrow & \lambda=2 \\ \\ \therefore & \text{Point A}=(5,1,8) \\ \\ \therefore & \text{Distance (AP)} \\ \\ = & \sqrt{(5+1)^{2}+(9-1)^{2}+(-16-8)^{2}} \\ \\ = & \sqrt{36+64+576} \\ \\ = & 26\text{units} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & A(-6,0,0)B(0,-2,0)C=(0,0,3) \\ \\ & \vec{AB}=6\hat{i}-2\hat{j},\vec{BC}=2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}, \\ \\ & \vec{AC}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{AH} \cdot \vec{BC}=0 \\ \\ & (\alpha+6,\beta,\frac{6}{7}) \cdot (0,2,3)=0 \\ \\ & \beta=\frac{-9}{7} \\ \\ & \vec{CH} \cdot \vec{AB}=0 \\ \\ & (\alpha,\beta,\frac{-15}{7}) \cdot (6,-2,0)=0 \\ \\ & 6\alpha-2\beta=0 \\ \\ & \alpha=\frac{-3}{7} \end{aligned}$ $98(\alpha+\beta)^{2}=(98)\frac{(144)}{49}=288$

questions.question_text: Let $P_{1}$ be the plane $3x-y-7z=11$ and $P_{2}$ be the plane passing through the points $(2,-1,0),(2,0,-1)$ , and $(5,1,1)$ . If the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $(7,4,-1)$ on the line of intersection of the planes $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ , then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ___________.
questions.question_html: Let $P_{1}$ be the plane $3x-y-7z=11$ and $P_{2}$ be the plane passing through the points $(2,-1,0),(2,0,-1)$ , and $(5,1,1)$ . If the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $(7,4,-1)$ on the line of intersection of the planes $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ , then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane $P_{2}$ passing through $(2,-1,0),(2,0$ , $-1)$ and $(5,1,1)$ is $\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} x-5 & y-1 & z-1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (x-5)(4-1)-(y-1)(6-3)+(z-1)(3-6)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 3x-15-3y+3-3z+3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 3x-3y-3z-9=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x-y-z=3.......(i) \end{aligned}$ Now, direction ratios of line of intersection of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ is $\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & -7 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\hat{i}(7-1)-\hat{j}(-7+3)+\hat{k}(-1+3) \\ \\ & =6\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ At $z=0,x-y=3$ [from (i)] $3x-y=11$ On solving, we get $x=4\text{and}y=1$ So, equation of line is $\frac{x-4}{6}=\frac{y-1}{4}=\frac{z-2}{6}=k$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(6k+4,4k+1,2k) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (6)(\alpha-7)+4(\beta-4)+2(\gamma+1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6(6k+4-7)+4(4k+1-4)+2(2k+1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 36k-18+16k-12+4k+4=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 56k=26 \Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ & \text{So,}\alpha=7,\beta=3\text{and}\gamma=1 \\ \\ & \therefore \alpha+\beta+\gamma=7+3+1=11 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-6}{2}$ and $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{1-y}{2}=\frac{z+8}{0}$ is equal to ________
questions.explanation_text: For $L_{1}:$ $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-6}{2}$ $\therefore$ Point on line is $A(2,-1,6)$ Parallel vector to this line is, $\vec{p}=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ For $L_{2}:$ $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z+8}{0}$ $\therefore$ Point on line is $B(6,1,-8)$ Parallel vector to this line is, $\vec{q}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+0\hat{k}$ Now shortest distance between this two lines is, $=|\frac{\vec{AB}.(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})}{|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|}|$ Now, $\vec{AB}=4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-14\hat{k}$ $\vec{p} \times \vec{q}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 0 \end{aligned}|$ $=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}-12\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|=\sqrt{16+36+144}=\sqrt{196}=14$ and $\vec{AB}.(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})=+16+12+168=+196$ $\therefore$ Shortest distance $=|\frac{196}{14}|=14$

$\vec{p}=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

For $L_{2}:$ $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z+8}{0}$

$\therefore$ Point on line is $B(6,1,-8)$

Parallel vector to this line is,

$\vec{q}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+0\hat{k}$

Now shortest distance between this two lines is,

$=|\frac{\vec{AB}.(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})}{|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|}|$

Now, $\vec{AB}=4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-14\hat{k}$

$\vec{p} \times \vec{q}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 0 \end{aligned}|$

$=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}-12\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ $|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|=\sqrt{16+36+144}=\sqrt{196}=14$

and $\vec{AB}.(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})=+16+12+168=+196$

$\therefore$ Shortest distance $=|\frac{196}{14}|=14$

questions.question_text: Let the system of linear equations $-x+2y-9z=7$ $-x+3y+7z=9$ $-2x+y+5z=8$ $-3x+y+13z=\lambda$ has a unique solution $x=\alpha,y=\beta,z=\gamma$ . Then the distance of the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=\lambda$ is :
questions.question_html:
Let the system of linear equations

$-x+2y-9z=7$

$-x+3y+7z=9$

$-2x+y+5z=8$

$-3x+y+13z=\lambda$

has a unique solution $x=\alpha,y=\beta,z=\gamma$ . Then the distance of the point

$(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=\lambda$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & -x+2y-9z=7-(1) \\ \\ & -x+3y-7z=9-(2) \\ \\ & -2x+y+5z=8-(3) \\ \\ & (2)-(1) \\ \\ & y+16z=2(4) \\ \\ & (3)-2 \times (1) \\ \\ & -3y+23z=-6-(5) \\ \\ & 3 \times (4)+(5) \\ \\ & 71z=0 \Rightarrow z=0 \\ \\ & y=2 \\ \\ & (-3,2,0) \rightarrow (\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \\ \\ & \text{Put in}-3x+y+13z=\lambda \\ \\ & \lambda=9+2=11 \end{aligned}$ The equation of the plane is: $2x-2y+z=\lambda$ We already know that $\lambda=11$ . So the equation of the plane becomes: $2x-2y+z=11$ Now, let's find the distance $d$ of the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(-3,2,0)$ from the plane using the formula : $d=\frac{|Ax+By+Cz+D|}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}+C^{2}}}$ Plugging in the values for the point and the plane equation, we get: $d=\frac{|2(-3)-2(2)+0-11|}{\sqrt{2^{2}+(-2)^{2}+1^{2}}}=\frac{|-6-4-11|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}}=\frac{21}{\sqrt{9}}=7$ So, the distance of the point $(-3,2,0)$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=11$ is 7.
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & -x+2y-9z=7-(1) \\ \\ & -x+3y-7z=9-(2) \\ \\ & -2x+y+5z=8-(3) \\ \\ & (2)-(1) \\ \\ & y+16z=2(4) \\ \\ & (3)-2 \times (1) \\ \\ & -3y+23z=-6-(5) \\ \\ & 3 \times (4)+(5) \\ \\ & 71z=0 \Rightarrow z=0 \\ \\ & y=2 \\ \\ & (-3,2,0) \rightarrow (\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \\ \\ & \text{Put in}-3x+y+13z=\lambda \\ \\ & \lambda=9+2=11 \end{aligned}$

The equation of the plane is:

$2x-2y+z=\lambda$

We already know that $\lambda=11$ . So the equation of the plane becomes:

$2x-2y+z=11$

Now, let's find the distance $d$ of the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(-3,2,0)$ from the plane using the formula :

$d=\frac{|Ax+By+Cz+D|}{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}+C^{2}}}$

Plugging in the values for the point and the plane equation, we get:

$d=\frac{|2(-3)-2(2)+0-11|}{\sqrt{2^{2}+(-2)^{2}+1^{2}}}=\frac{|-6-4-11|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}}=\frac{21}{\sqrt{9}}=7$

So, the distance of the point $(-3,2,0)$ from the plane $2x-2y+z=11$ is 7.

questions.question_html: Let $N$ be the foot of perpendicular from the point $P(1,-2,3)$ on the line passing through the points $(4,5,8)$ and $(1,-7,5)$ . Then the distance of $N$ from the plane $2x-2y+z+5=0$ is :
questions.explanation_text:
Equation of line $\frac{x-4}{4-1}=\frac{y-5}{5-(-7)}=\frac{z-8}{8-5}$ $\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-5}{12}=\frac{z-8}{3}$ Let point $N(3\lambda+4,12\lambda+5,3\lambda+8)$ $\vec{PN}=(3\lambda+4-1)\hat{i}+(12\lambda+5-(-2))\hat{j}+(3\lambda+8-3)\hat{k}$ $\vec{PN}=(3\lambda+3)\hat{i}+(12\lambda+7)\hat{j}+(3\lambda+5)\hat{k}$ And parallel vector to line (say $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+12\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ ) Now, $\vec{PN} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ $\begin{aligned} & (3\lambda+3)3+(12\lambda+7)12+(3\lambda+5)3=0 \\ \\ & 162\lambda+108=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-108}{162}=\frac{-2}{3} \end{aligned}$ So point $N$ is $(2,-3,6)$ Now distance of
N(2, -3, 6) from $2x-2y+z+5=0$ is $=|\frac{2(2)-2(-3)+6+5}{\sqrt{4+4+1}}|=7$

$\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-5}{12}=\frac{z-8}{3}$

$\vec{PN}=(3\lambda+4-1)\hat{i}+(12\lambda+5-(-2))\hat{j}+(3\lambda+8-3)\hat{k}$

$\vec{PN}=(3\lambda+3)\hat{i}+(12\lambda+7)\hat{j}+(3\lambda+5)\hat{k}$

And parallel vector to line (say $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+12\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ )

Now, $\vec{PN} \cdot \vec{a}=0$

questions.question_text: Let two vertices of a triangle ABC be (2, 4, 6) and (0, $-$ 2, $-$ 5), and its centroid be (2, 1, $-$ 1). If the image of the third vertex in the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ , then $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let two vertices of a triangle ABC be (2, 4, 6) and (0, $-$ 2, $-$ 5), and its centroid be (2, 1, $-$ 1). If the image of the third vertex in the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ , then $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given that two vertex of a $△ABC$ be $A(2,4,6)$ and $B(0,-2,-5)$ and $G=$ centroid $=(2,1,-1)$ [Given] Let, the other vertex is $C(x,y,z)$ According to the question, $\begin{aligned} & \frac{2+0+x}{3}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=4 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{4-2+y}{3}=1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=1 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{6-5+z}{3}=-1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow z=1 \end{aligned}$ Hence, third vertex is $C(4,1,-4)$ Now, if image of $C(4,1,-4)$ in the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ is $D(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ . So, $\frac{\alpha-4}{1}=\frac{\beta-1}{2}=\frac{\gamma+4}{4}=k$ (say) $\Rightarrow \alpha=k+4,\beta=2k+1,\gamma=4k-4$ Then, co-ordinates of $D$ is $(k+4,2k+1,4k-4)$ Let, $E$ be the mid-point of $CD$ , which lies on the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ . Then, co-ordinates of $E$ is $(\frac{k+8}{2},\frac{2k+2}{2},\frac{4k-8}{2})=(\frac{k+8}{2},k+1,2k-4)$ Since, $E$ lies on the plane, $x+2y+4z-11=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\frac{k+8}{2}+2k+2+8k-16-11=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{k+8+4k+4+16k-54}{2}=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 21k=42 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow k=2 \end{aligned}$ Hence, $D \equiv (6,5,4) \equiv (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ So, $\alpha=6,\beta=5,\gamma=4$ Now, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=6 \times 5+5 \times 4+4 \times 6$ $=30+20+24=74$
questions.explanation_html:
Given that two vertex of a $△ABC$ be $A(2,4,6)$ and

$B(0,-2,-5)$ and $G=$ centroid $=(2,1,-1)$ [Given]

Let, the other vertex is $C(x,y,z)$

According to the question,

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{2+0+x}{3}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=4 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{4-2+y}{3}=1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=1 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{6-5+z}{3}=-1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow z=1 \end{aligned}$

Hence, third vertex is $C(4,1,-4)$

Now, if image of $C(4,1,-4)$ in the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ is $D(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ .

So, $\frac{\alpha-4}{1}=\frac{\beta-1}{2}=\frac{\gamma+4}{4}=k$ (say)



$\Rightarrow \alpha=k+4,\beta=2k+1,\gamma=4k-4$

Then, co-ordinates of $D$ is $(k+4,2k+1,4k-4)$

Let, $E$ be the mid-point of $CD$ , which lies on the plane $x+2y+4z=11$ .

Then, co-ordinates of $E$ is

$(\frac{k+8}{2},\frac{2k+2}{2},\frac{4k-8}{2})=(\frac{k+8}{2},k+1,2k-4)$

Since, $E$ lies on the plane, $x+2y+4z-11=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\frac{k+8}{2}+2k+2+8k-16-11=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{k+8+4k+4+16k-54}{2}=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 21k=42 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow k=2 \end{aligned}$

Hence, $D \equiv (6,5,4) \equiv (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$



So, $\alpha=6,\beta=5,\gamma=4$

Now, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=6 \times 5+5 \times 4+4 \times 6$

$=30+20+24=74$

questions.question_text: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-4}{4}=\frac{y+2}{5}=\frac{z+3}{3}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ is :
questions.question_html: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-4}{4}=\frac{y+2}{5}=\frac{z+3}{3}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: The given lines are $\frac{x-4}{4}=\frac{y+2}{5}=\frac{z+3}{3}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\vec{b}_{1}=4\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}_{2}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{1}=4\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{2}=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 & 2 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =(10-12)\hat{i}-(8-9)\hat{j}+(16-15)\hat{k} \\ \\ & =-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Shortest distance,}d=|\frac{(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}-7\hat{k}) \cdot (-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})}{\sqrt{4+1+1}}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{-6-5-7}{\sqrt{6}}|=\frac{18}{\sqrt{6}}=3\sqrt{6}\text{units} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
The given lines are

$\frac{x-4}{4}=\frac{y+2}{5}=\frac{z+3}{3}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-4}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\vec{b}_{1}=4\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}_{2}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{1}=4\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{2}=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 & 2 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =(10-12)\hat{i}-(8-9)\hat{j}+(16-15)\hat{k} \\ \\ & =-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Shortest distance,}d=|\frac{(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}-7\hat{k}) \cdot (-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})}{\sqrt{4+1+1}}| \\ \\ & =|\frac{-6-5-7}{\sqrt{6}}|=\frac{18}{\sqrt{6}}=3\sqrt{6}\text{units} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane intersection of two plane $P_{1}+\lambda P_{2}=0$ $P_{1}:2x-y+z=3,\text{and}P_{2}:4x-3y+5z+9=0$ Equation of any plane passing through the intersection of given planes is $(2x-y+z-3)+\lambda(4x-3y+5z+9)=0$ $\Rightarrow (2+4\lambda)x+(-1-3\lambda)y+(1+5\lambda)z+(-3+9\lambda)=0$ ..........(i) Plane (i) is parallel to given line $\begin{aligned} & \therefore (-2)(2+4\lambda)+4(-1-3\lambda)+5(1+5\lambda)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4-8\lambda-4-12\lambda+5+25\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 5\lambda-3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$ Putting the value of $\lambda$ in Eq. (i), we get $\begin{aligned} & (2x-y+z-3)+\frac{3}{5}(4x-3y+5z+9)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 11x-7y+10z+6=0 \\ \\ & \therefore a=11,b=-7,c=10\text{and}d=6 \\ \\ & \therefore a+b+c=11-7+10=14 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of plane intersection of two plane

$P_{1}+\lambda P_{2}=0$

$P_{1}:2x-y+z=3,\text{and}P_{2}:4x-3y+5z+9=0$

Equation of any plane passing through the intersection of given planes is

$(2x-y+z-3)+\lambda(4x-3y+5z+9)=0$

$\Rightarrow (2+4\lambda)x+(-1-3\lambda)y+(1+5\lambda)z+(-3+9\lambda)=0$ ..........(i)

Plane (i) is parallel to given line

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore (-2)(2+4\lambda)+4(-1-3\lambda)+5(1+5\lambda)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4-8\lambda-4-12\lambda+5+25\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 5\lambda-3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$

Putting the value of $\lambda$ in Eq. (i), we get

$\begin{aligned} & (2x-y+z-3)+\frac{3}{5}(4x-3y+5z+9)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 11x-7y+10z+6=0 \\ \\ & \therefore a=11,b=-7,c=10\text{and}d=6 \\ \\ & \therefore a+b+c=11-7+10=14 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Point $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ lies on the plane $2x+4y+3z=5$ , $\therefore$ $2\alpha+4\beta+3\gamma=5$ ........(1) Given, $(\begin{aligned} \alpha & \beta & \gamma \end{aligned})⎛⎝⎜\begin{aligned} 2 & 10 & 8 \\ 9 & 3 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 & 8 \end{aligned}⎞⎠⎟=(\begin{aligned} 0 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned})$ $\therefore$ $2\alpha+9\beta+8\gamma=0$ .......(2) and $10\alpha+3\beta+4\gamma=0$ ........(3) and $8\alpha+8\beta+8\gamma=0$ ..........(4) Subtract (4) from (2) $-6\alpha+\beta=0$ $\beta=6\alpha$ From equation (4) $8\alpha+48\alpha+8\gamma=0$ $\gamma=-7\alpha$ From equation (1) $2\alpha+24\alpha-21\alpha=5$ $5\alpha=5$ $\alpha=1$ $\beta=+6,\gamma=-7$ $\therefore 6\alpha+9\beta+7\gamma$ $=6+54-49$ $=11$

$\therefore$ $2\alpha+4\beta+3\gamma=5$ ........(1)

and $10\alpha+3\beta+4\gamma=0$ ........(3)

and $8\alpha+8\beta+8\gamma=0$ ..........(4)

Subtract (4) from (2)

$-6\alpha+\beta=0$ $\beta=6\alpha$

From equation (4)

$8\alpha+48\alpha+8\gamma=0$

$\gamma=-7\alpha$

From equation (1)

$2\alpha+24\alpha-21\alpha=5$

$5\alpha=5$

$\alpha=1$

$\beta=+6,\gamma=-7$

$\therefore 6\alpha+9\beta+7\gamma$

$=6+54-49$

$=11$

$\begin{aligned} & P(2\lambda-1,5\lambda+1,-\lambda-1) \\ \\ & \vec{PA}=(3-2\lambda)\hat{i}-(5\lambda+1)\hat{j}+(6+\lambda)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \text{Direction ratio of line} \Rightarrow \vec{b}=2\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \text{Now,} \Rightarrow \vec{PA} \cdot \vec{b}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2(3-2\lambda)-5(5\lambda+1)-(6+\lambda)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-1}{6} \\ \\ & P(2\lambda-1,5\lambda+1,-\lambda-1) \equiv P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=2(-\frac{1}{6})-1=-\frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \alpha=-\frac{4}{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \beta=5(-\frac{1}{6})+1=\frac{1}{6} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{1}{6} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \gamma=-\lambda-1=\frac{1}{6}-1 \Rightarrow \gamma=-\frac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}$ be the values of $\lambda$ for which the points $(\frac{5}{2},1,\lambda)$ and $(-2,0,1)$ are at equal distance from the plane $2x+3y-6z+7=0$ . If $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}$ , then the distance of the point $(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{1})$ from the line $\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+7}{2}$ is ____________.
questions.question_html: Let $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}$ be the values of $\lambda$ for which the points $(\frac{5}{2},1,\lambda)$ and $(-2,0,1)$ are at equal distance from the plane $2x+3y-6z+7=0$ . If $\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}$ , then the distance of the point $(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{1})$ from the line $\frac{x-5}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+7}{2}$ is ____________.
questions.explanation_text: Since $(\frac{5}{2},1,\lambda)$ and $(-2,0,1)$ are equidistant from plane $2x+3y-6z+7=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore |\frac{2(\frac{5}{2})+3(1)-6(\lambda)+7}{\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}}|=|\frac{2(-2)+3(0)-6(1)+7}{\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |5+3-6\lambda+7|=|-4-6+7| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |15-6\lambda|=|-3| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 15-6\lambda= \pm 3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 15-6\lambda=3\text{or}15-6\lambda=-3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6\lambda=12\text{or}6\lambda=18 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=2\text{or}\lambda=3 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \because \lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2} \\ \\ & \therefore \lambda_{1}=3\text{and}\lambda_{2}=2 \end{aligned}$ So, point will be $(1,2,3)$ Let $M_{0}=(1,2,3)$ $M_{1}$ is the point through which line passes i.e, $(5,1,-7)$ and $\vec{s}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\therefore \vec{M_{0}M_{1}}=4\hat{i}-\hat{j}-10\hat{k}$ Now, required distance $=|\frac{\vec{M_{0}M_{1}} \times \vec{s}}{|\vec{s}|}|$ $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{|(4\hat{i}-\hat{j}-10\hat{k}) \times (\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\ \\ & =\frac{|18\hat{i}-18\hat{j}+9\hat{k}|}{3}=9 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Since $(\frac{5}{2},1,\lambda)$ and $(-2,0,1)$ are equidistant

from plane $2x+3y-6z+7=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore |\frac{2(\frac{5}{2})+3(1)-6(\lambda)+7}{\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}}|=|\frac{2(-2)+3(0)-6(1)+7}{\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |5+3-6\lambda+7|=|-4-6+7| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |15-6\lambda|=|-3| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 15-6\lambda= \pm 3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 15-6\lambda=3\text{or}15-6\lambda=-3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6\lambda=12\text{or}6\lambda=18 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=2\text{or}\lambda=3 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \because \lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2} \\ \\ & \therefore \lambda_{1}=3\text{and}\lambda_{2}=2 \end{aligned}$

So, point will be $(1,2,3)$

Let $M_{0}=(1,2,3)$

$M_{1}$ is the point through which line passes i.e, $(5,1,-7)$

and $\vec{s}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\therefore \vec{M_{0}M_{1}}=4\hat{i}-\hat{j}-10\hat{k}$

Now, required distance $=|\frac{\vec{M_{0}M_{1}} \times \vec{s}}{|\vec{s}|}|$

$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{|(4\hat{i}-\hat{j}-10\hat{k}) \times (\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\ \\ & =\frac{|18\hat{i}-18\hat{j}+9\hat{k}|}{3}=9 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: If the equation of the plane passing through the point $(1,1,2)$ and perpendicular to the line $x-3y+2z-1=0=4x-y+z$ is $Ax+By+Cz=1$ , then $140(C-B+A)$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: Line of intersection of the planes $x-3y+2z-1=0$ and $4x-y+z=0$ is normal $(\vec{n})$ to the required plane. $\vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 4 & -1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$ Equation of plane is $-x+7y+11z=\lambda$ It passes through (1, 1, 2) $\therefore$ $\lambda=28$ So, the plane is $-x+7y+11z=28$ $\Rightarrow \frac{-1}{28}x+\frac{7}{28}y+\frac{11}{28}z=1$ $A=\frac{-1}{28},B=\frac{7}{28},C=\frac{11}{28}$ $140(C-B+A)=15$
questions.explanation_html:
Line of intersection of the planes $x-3y+2z-1=0$ and $4x-y+z=0$ is normal $(\vec{n})$ to the required plane.

$\vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 4 & -1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$

Equation of plane is

$-x+7y+11z=\lambda$

It passes through (1, 1, 2)

$\therefore$ $\lambda=28$

So, the plane is

$-x+7y+11z=28$

$\Rightarrow \frac{-1}{28}x+\frac{7}{28}y+\frac{11}{28}z=1$

$A=\frac{-1}{28},B=\frac{7}{28},C=\frac{11}{28}$

$140(C-B+A)=15$

questions.question_text: Let $S$ be the set of all values of $\lambda$ , for which the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{0}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z+6}{1}$ and $\frac{x+\lambda}{3}=\frac{y}{-4}=\frac{z-6}{0}$ is 13. Then $8|\underset{\lambda \in S}{\sum}\lambda|$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $S$ be the set of all values of $\lambda$ , for which the shortest distance between

the lines $\frac{x-\lambda}{0}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z+6}{1}$ and $\frac{x+\lambda}{3}=\frac{y}{-4}=\frac{z-6}{0}$ is 13. Then $8|\underset{\lambda \in S}{\sum}\lambda|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given the two lines : $\frac{x-\lambda}{0}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z+6}{1}\frac{x+\lambda}{3}=\frac{y}{-4}=\frac{z-6}{0}$ Let's find the direction vectors of these lines: $\vec{d_{1}}=⟨0,4,1⟩$ and $\vec{d_{2}}=⟨3,-4,0⟩$ . Now, let's find the cross product of the direction vectors, which will give a vector that is perpendicular to both lines : $\vec{n}=\vec{d_{1}} \times \vec{d_{2}}=⟨4,3,-12⟩$ Let's find the vector connecting a point on line 1 to a point on line 2 : $\vec{c}=⟨2\lambda,3,-12⟩$ The shortest distance between the two lines is the projection of $\vec{c}$ onto $\vec{n}$ : $d=|\frac{\vec{c} \cdot \vec{n}}{|\vec{n}|}|=|\frac{(2\lambda)(4)+(3)(3)-(12)(-12)}{\sqrt{16+9+144}}|$ We are given that the shortest distance is 13 : $13=|\frac{8\lambda+153}{13}|$ $|8\lambda+153|=169$ We have two cases : 1. $8\lambda+153=169$ $\lambda=\frac{16}{8}$ 2. $8\lambda+153=-169$ $\lambda=\frac{-322}{8}$ Now, let's calculate $8|\underset{\lambda \in S}{\sum}\lambda|$ : $8|\frac{16}{8}+\frac{-322}{8}|=8|\frac{-306}{8}|=306$ Thus, the correct answer is Option A : 306.
questions.explanation_html:
Given the two lines :

$\frac{x-\lambda}{0}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z+6}{1}\frac{x+\lambda}{3}=\frac{y}{-4}=\frac{z-6}{0}$

Let's find the direction vectors of these lines: $\vec{d_{1}}=⟨0,4,1⟩$ and $\vec{d_{2}}=⟨3,-4,0⟩$ .

Now, let's find the cross product of the direction vectors, which will give a vector that is perpendicular to both lines :

$\vec{n}=\vec{d_{1}} \times \vec{d_{2}}=⟨4,3,-12⟩$

Let's find the vector connecting a point on line 1 to a point on line 2 :

$\vec{c}=⟨2\lambda,3,-12⟩$

The shortest distance between the two lines is the projection of $\vec{c}$ onto $\vec{n}$ :

$d=|\frac{\vec{c} \cdot \vec{n}}{|\vec{n}|}|=|\frac{(2\lambda)(4)+(3)(3)-(12)(-12)}{\sqrt{16+9+144}}|$

We are given that the shortest distance is 13 :

$13=|\frac{8\lambda+153}{13}|$

$|8\lambda+153|=169$

We have two cases :

1. $8\lambda+153=169$

$\lambda=\frac{16}{8}$

2. $8\lambda+153=-169$

$\lambda=\frac{-322}{8}$

Now, let's calculate $8|\underset{\lambda \in S}{\sum}\lambda|$ :

$8|\frac{16}{8}+\frac{-322}{8}|=8|\frac{-306}{8}|=306$

Thus, the correct answer is Option A : 306.

questions.question_text: Let the equation of plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $x+2y+az=2$ and $x-y+z=3$ be $5x-11y+bz=6a-1$ . For $c \in ℤ$ , if the distance of this plane from the point $(a,-c,c)$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{a}}$ , then $\frac{a+b}{c}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the equation of plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $x+2y+az=2$ and $x-y+z=3$ be $5x-11y+bz=6a-1$ . For $c \in ℤ$ , if the distance of this plane from the point $(a,-c,c)$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{a}}$ , then $\frac{a+b}{c}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given the equation of the plane passing through the intersection of the two given planes: $P:(x+2y+az-2)+\lambda(x-y+z-3)=0$ $\Rightarrow x(\lambda+1)+y(2-\lambda)+z(a+\lambda)-2-3\lambda=0$ This is the same as the given equation $5x-11y+bz=6a-1$ . Now, comparing the coefficients of the corresponding variables in both equations: $\frac{\lambda+1}{5}=\frac{2-\lambda}{-11}=\frac{a+\lambda}{b}=\frac{2+3\lambda}{6a-1}$ Solving for $\lambda$ : $-11\lambda-11=10-5\lambda$ $6\lambda=-21 \Rightarrow \lambda=-\frac{7}{2}$ Now, substituting the value of $\lambda$ back into the equations: $\frac{2-\lambda}{-11}=\frac{2+3\lambda}{6a-1} \Rightarrow \frac{2+\frac{7}{2}}{-11}=\frac{2-\frac{21}{2}}{6a-1}$ From this equation, we find the value of a : $6a-1=17 \Rightarrow a=3$ Now, substituting the value of $a$ and $\lambda$ into the equation: $\frac{2-\lambda}{-11}=\frac{a+\lambda}{b} \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3-\frac{7}{2}}{b}$ $\Rightarrow -\frac{b}{2}=-\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow b=1$ Therefore, the point $(a,-c,c) \equiv (3,-c,c)$ . The given distance is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{a}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ . The plane is: $5x-11y+z=17$ . Now, let's find the distance: $|\frac{15+11c+c-17}{\sqrt{147}}|=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\Rightarrow c=-1,\frac{4}{3}$ Since $c \in ℤ$ , we have $c=-1$ . Therefore, $\frac{a+b}{c}=\frac{3+1}{-1}=-4$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given the equation of the plane passing through the intersection of the two given planes:

$P:(x+2y+az-2)+\lambda(x-y+z-3)=0$

$\Rightarrow x(\lambda+1)+y(2-\lambda)+z(a+\lambda)-2-3\lambda=0$

This is the same as the given equation $5x-11y+bz=6a-1$ .

Now, comparing the coefficients of the corresponding variables in both equations:

$\frac{\lambda+1}{5}=\frac{2-\lambda}{-11}=\frac{a+\lambda}{b}=\frac{2+3\lambda}{6a-1}$

Solving for $\lambda$ :

$-11\lambda-11=10-5\lambda$

$6\lambda=-21 \Rightarrow \lambda=-\frac{7}{2}$

Now, substituting the value of $\lambda$ back into the equations:

$\frac{2-\lambda}{-11}=\frac{2+3\lambda}{6a-1} \Rightarrow \frac{2+\frac{7}{2}}{-11}=\frac{2-\frac{21}{2}}{6a-1}$

From this equation, we find the value of a :

$6a-1=17 \Rightarrow a=3$

Now, substituting the value of $a$ and $\lambda$ into the equation:

$\frac{2-\lambda}{-11}=\frac{a+\lambda}{b} \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3-\frac{7}{2}}{b}$

$\Rightarrow -\frac{b}{2}=-\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow b=1$

Therefore, the point $(a,-c,c) \equiv (3,-c,c)$ .

The given distance is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{a}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ .

The plane is: $5x-11y+z=17$ .

Now, let's find the distance:

$|\frac{15+11c+c-17}{\sqrt{147}}|=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\Rightarrow c=-1,\frac{4}{3}$

Since $c \in ℤ$ , we have $c=-1$ .

Therefore, $\frac{a+b}{c}=\frac{3+1}{-1}=-4$ .

questions.question_text: Let the line passing through the points $P(2,-1,2)$ and $Q(5,3,4)$ meet the plane $x-y+z=4$ at the point $R$ . Then the distance of the point $R$ from the plane $x+2y+3z+2=0$ measured parallel to the line $\frac{x-7}{2}=\frac{y+3}{2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the line passing through the points $P(2,-1,2)$ and $Q(5,3,4)$ meet the plane $x-y+z=4$ at the point $R$ . Then the distance of the point $R$ from the plane $x+2y+3z+2=0$ measured parallel to the line $\frac{x-7}{2}=\frac{y+3}{2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of line $PQ$ : $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{4}=\frac{z-2}{2}=\lambda$ Let $R$ be $(3\lambda+2,4\lambda-1,2\lambda+2)$ $R$ lies on plane $x-y+z=4$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 3\lambda+2-4\lambda+1+2\lambda+2=4 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=-1 \\ \\ & \therefore R(-1,-5,0) \end{aligned}$ $\text{Let}SR\text{be}:\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y+5}{2}=\frac{z-0}{1}=k$ Point $S:(2k-1,2k-5,k)$ $S$ lies on plane: $x+2y+3z+2=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (2k-1)+(4k-10)+3k+2=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 9k-9=0 \Rightarrow k=1 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore S=(1,-3,1)$ $\therefore SR=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of line $PQ$ :

$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{4}=\frac{z-2}{2}=\lambda$

Let $R$ be $(3\lambda+2,4\lambda-1,2\lambda+2)$

$R$ lies on plane $x-y+z=4$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore 3\lambda+2-4\lambda+1+2\lambda+2=4 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=-1 \\ \\ & \therefore R(-1,-5,0) \end{aligned}$

$\text{Let}SR\text{be}:\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y+5}{2}=\frac{z-0}{1}=k$



Point $S:(2k-1,2k-5,k)$

$S$ lies on plane: $x+2y+3z+2=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (2k-1)+(4k-10)+3k+2=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 9k-9=0 \Rightarrow k=1 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore S=(1,-3,1)$

$\therefore SR=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3$
