questions.question_text: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,6)$ in the plane passing through the points $A(1,2,0),B(1,4,1)$ and $C(0,5,1)$ be $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ . Then $(\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2})$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,6)$ in the plane passing through the points $A(1,2,0),B(1,4,1)$ and $C(0,5,1)$ be $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ . Then $(\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane passing through the points $A(1,2$ , $0),B(1,4,1)$ and $C(0,5,1)$ is $\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} x-1 & y-2 & z-0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x+y-2z=3 \end{aligned}$ Now $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the image of the point $P(1,2,6)$ in the plane $x+y-2z-3=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\alpha-1}{1}=\frac{\beta-2}{1}=\frac{\gamma-6}{-2}=\frac{-2[1+2-2(6)-3]}{1^{2}+1^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\alpha-1}{1}=\frac{\beta-2}{1}=\frac{\gamma-6}{-2}=4 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=5,\beta=6,\gamma=-2 \end{aligned}$ $\text{Hence,}\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}=5^{2}+6^{2}+(-2)^{2}=65$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of plane passing through the points $A(1,2$ , $0),B(1,4,1)$ and $C(0,5,1)$ is

$\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} x-1 & y-2 & z-0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x+y-2z=3 \end{aligned}$

Now $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the image of the point $P(1,2,6)$ in the plane $x+y-2z-3=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\alpha-1}{1}=\frac{\beta-2}{1}=\frac{\gamma-6}{-2}=\frac{-2[1+2-2(6)-3]}{1^{2}+1^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\alpha-1}{1}=\frac{\beta-2}{1}=\frac{\gamma-6}{-2}=4 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=5,\beta=6,\gamma=-2 \end{aligned}$

$\text{Hence,}\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}=5^{2}+6^{2}+(-2)^{2}=65$

questions.question_text: Let P be the point of intersection of the line $\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{1-z}{2}$ and the plane $x+y+z=2$ . If the distance of the point P from the plane $3x-4y+12z=32$ is q, then q and 2q are the roots of the equation :
questions.question_html: Let P be the point of intersection of the line $\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{1-z}{2}$ and the plane $x+y+z=2$ . If the distance of the point P from the plane $3x-4y+12z=32$ is q, then q and 2q are the roots of the equation :
questions.explanation_text: Given, equation of line is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{1-z}{2}=k \\ \\ & \therefore x=3k-3,y=k-2,z=1-2k \end{aligned}$ Since, given that $P \equiv (3k-3,k-2,1-2k)$ be the point of intersection of the given line and the plane $x+y+z=2$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}(3k-3)+(k-2)+(1-2k)=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2k-4=2 \Rightarrow k=3 \end{aligned}$ Thus, $P=(6,1,-5)$ Now, distance of point $P$ from the plane $3x-4y+12z=32$ is $\begin{aligned} & q=|\frac{18-4-60-32}{\sqrt{9+16+144}}|=|\frac{-78}{\sqrt{169}}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow q=|\frac{-78}{13}|=\frac{78}{13}=6 \\ \\ & \therefore q=6 \Rightarrow 2q=12 \end{aligned}$ Thus, $q$ and $2q$ are roots of the equation $x^{2}-18x+72=0$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, equation of line is

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y+2}{1}=\frac{1-z}{2}=k \\ \\ & \therefore x=3k-3,y=k-2,z=1-2k \end{aligned}$

Since, given that $P \equiv (3k-3,k-2,1-2k)$ be the point of intersection of the given line and the plane $x+y+z=2$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}(3k-3)+(k-2)+(1-2k)=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2k-4=2 \Rightarrow k=3 \end{aligned}$

Thus, $P=(6,1,-5)$

Now, distance of point $P$ from the plane $3x-4y+12z=32$ is

$\begin{aligned} & q=|\frac{18-4-60-32}{\sqrt{9+16+144}}|=|\frac{-78}{\sqrt{169}}| \\ \\ & \Rightarrow q=|\frac{-78}{13}|=\frac{78}{13}=6 \\ \\ & \therefore q=6 \Rightarrow 2q=12 \end{aligned}$

Thus, $q$ and $2q$ are roots of the equation $x^{2}-18x+72=0$

questions.question_text: If the equation of the plane containing the line $x+2y+3z-4=0=2x+y-z+5$ and perpendicular to the plane $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ is $ax+by+cz=4$ , then $(a-b+c)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
If the equation of the plane containing the line

$x+2y+3z-4=0=2x+y-z+5$ and perpendicular to the plane

$\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$

is $ax+by+cz=4$ , then $(a-b+c)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane $P$ containing the given lines is $\begin{aligned} & (x+2y+3z-4)+\lambda(2x+y-z+5)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (1+2\lambda)x+(2+\lambda)y+(3-\lambda)z+(-4+5\lambda)=0 \end{aligned}$ Now, plane $P$ is perpendicular to plane $P^{'}$ $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ So, normal to plane $P^{'}$ is $\begin{aligned} & \vec{n}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \times (\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{n}=5\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore P$ and $P^{'}$ are perpendicular $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 5(1+2\lambda)-2(2+\lambda)-3(3-\lambda)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 5+10\lambda-4-2\lambda-9+3\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 11\lambda=8 \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{8}{11} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \therefore P:(1+\frac{16}{11})x+(2+\frac{8}{11})y+(3-\frac{8}{11})z+(5 \times \frac{8}{11}-4)=0 \end{aligned}$ i.e., $27x+30y+25z=4$ which is same as $ax+by+cz=4$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore a=27,b=30\text{and}c=25 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a-b+c=27-30+25=22 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of plane $P$ containing the given lines is

$\begin{aligned} & (x+2y+3z-4)+\lambda(2x+y-z+5)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (1+2\lambda)x+(2+\lambda)y+(3-\lambda)z+(-4+5\lambda)=0 \end{aligned}$

Now, plane $P$ is perpendicular to plane $P^{'}$

$\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$

So, normal to plane $P^{'}$ is

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{n}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \times (\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{n}=5\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore P$ and $P^{'}$ are perpendicular

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore 5(1+2\lambda)-2(2+\lambda)-3(3-\lambda)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 5+10\lambda-4-2\lambda-9+3\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 11\lambda=8 \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{8}{11} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \therefore P:(1+\frac{16}{11})x+(2+\frac{8}{11})y+(3-\frac{8}{11})z+(5 \times \frac{8}{11}-4)=0 \end{aligned}$

i.e., $27x+30y+25z=4$

which is same as $ax+by+cz=4$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore a=27,b=30\text{and}c=25 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a-b+c=27-30+25=22 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: One vertex of a rectangular parallelopiped is at the origin $O$ and the lengths of its edges along $x,y$ and $z$ axes are $3,4$ and $5$ units respectively. Let $P$ be the vertex $(3,4,5)$ . Then the shortest distance between the diagonal OP and an edge parallel to $z$ axis, not passing through $O$ or $P$ is :
questions.question_html: One vertex of a rectangular parallelopiped is at the origin $O$ and the lengths of its edges along $x,y$ and $z$ axes are $3,4$ and $5$ units respectively. Let $P$ be the vertex $(3,4,5)$ . Then the shortest distance between the diagonal OP and an edge parallel to $z$ axis, not passing through $O$ or $P$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of $OP$ is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{x-0}{3-0}=\frac{y-0}{4-0}=\frac{z-0}{5-0} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{x}{3}=\frac{y}{4}=\frac{z}{5} \end{aligned}$ Equation of edge parallel to $Z$ -axis is $\frac{x-3}{0}=\frac{y-0}{0}=\frac{z-5}{1}$ $\therefore$ Shortest distance $=\frac{|\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|}{\sqrt{\begin{aligned} (a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1})^{2}+(b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1})^{2}+(c_{1}a_{2}-c_{2}a_{1})^{2} \end{aligned}}}$ Here, $\begin{aligned} & x_{1}=0,y_{1}=0,z_{1}=0 \\ \\ & x_{2}=3,y_{2}=0,z_{2}=5 \\ \\ & a_{1}=3,b_{1}=4,c_{1}=5 \\ \\ & a_{2}=0,b_{2}=0,c_{2}=1 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore |\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned} 3 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|=4(3)=12$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{and}\sqrt{(a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1})^{2}+(b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1})^{2}+(c_{1}a_{2}-c_{2}a_{1})^{2}} \\ \\ & =\sqrt{0+(4-0)^{2}+(0-3)^{2}} \\ \\ & =\sqrt{16+9}=5 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Required shortest distance}=\frac{12}{5} \\ \\ & \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of $OP$ is

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x-0}{3-0}=\frac{y-0}{4-0}=\frac{z-0}{5-0} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{x}{3}=\frac{y}{4}=\frac{z}{5} \end{aligned}$

Equation of edge parallel to $Z$ -axis is

$\frac{x-3}{0}=\frac{y-0}{0}=\frac{z-5}{1}$

$\therefore$ Shortest distance

$=\frac{|\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|}{\sqrt{\begin{aligned} (a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1})^{2}+(b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1})^{2}+(c_{1}a_{2}-c_{2}a_{1})^{2} \end{aligned}}}$

Here,

$\begin{aligned} & x_{1}=0,y_{1}=0,z_{1}=0 \\ \\ & x_{2}=3,y_{2}=0,z_{2}=5 \\ \\ & a_{1}=3,b_{1}=4,c_{1}=5 \\ \\ & a_{2}=0,b_{2}=0,c_{2}=1 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore |\begin{aligned} x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned} 3 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|=4(3)=12$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{and}\sqrt{(a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1})^{2}+(b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1})^{2}+(c_{1}a_{2}-c_{2}a_{1})^{2}} \\ \\ & =\sqrt{0+(4-0)^{2}+(0-3)^{2}} \\ \\ & =\sqrt{16+9}=5 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Required shortest distance}=\frac{12}{5} \\ \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text:
Let the plane $P:8x+\alpha_{1}y+\alpha_{2}z+12=0$ be parallel to the line $L:\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+4}{5}$ . If the

intercept of $P$ on the $y$ -axis is 1 , then the distance between $P$ and $L$ is :
questions.question_html:
Let the plane $P:8x+\alpha_{1}y+\alpha_{2}z+12=0$ be parallel to

the line $L:\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+4}{5}$ . If the intercept of $P$

on the $y$ -axis is 1 , then the distance between $P$ and $L$ is :
questions.explanation_text: P: $8x+\alpha_{1}y+\alpha_{2}z+12=0$ L: $\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+4}{5}$ $\because P$ is parallel to $L$ $\Rightarrow 8(2)+\alpha_{1}(3)+5(\alpha_{2})=0$ $\Rightarrow 3\alpha_{1}+5(\alpha_{2})=-16$ Also $y$ -intercept of plane $P$ is 1 $\Rightarrow \alpha_{1}=-12$ And $\alpha_{2}=4$ $\Rightarrow$ Equation of plane $P$ is $2x-3y+z+3=0$ $\Rightarrow$ Distance of line L from Plane $P$ is $=|\frac{0-3(6)+1+3}{\sqrt{4+9+1}}|$ $=\sqrt{14}$
questions.explanation_html:
P: $8x+\alpha_{1}y+\alpha_{2}z+12=0$

L: $\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+4}{5}$

$\because P$ is parallel to $L$

$\Rightarrow 8(2)+\alpha_{1}(3)+5(\alpha_{2})=0$

$\Rightarrow 3\alpha_{1}+5(\alpha_{2})=-16$

Also $y$ -intercept of plane $P$ is 1

$\Rightarrow \alpha_{1}=-12$

And $\alpha_{2}=4$

$\Rightarrow$ Equation of plane $P$ is $2x-3y+z+3=0$

$\Rightarrow$ Distance of line L from Plane $P$ is

$=|\frac{0-3(6)+1+3}{\sqrt{4+9+1}}|$ $=\sqrt{14}$

questions.question_text: Let the shortest distance between the lines $L:\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-\lambda}{0}=\frac{z+\lambda}{1},\lambda \ge 0$ and $L_{1}:x+1=y-1=4-z$ be $2\sqrt{6}$ . If $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ lies on $L$ , then which of the following is NOT possible?
questions.question_html:
Let the shortest distance between the lines

$L:\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-\lambda}{0}=\frac{z+\lambda}{1},\lambda \ge 0$ and

$L_{1}:x+1=y-1=4-z$ be $2\sqrt{6}$ . If $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ lies on $L$ ,

then which of the following is NOT possible?
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-\lambda}{0}=\frac{z+\lambda}{1},\lambda \ge 0$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-4}{-1} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{1}=5\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}-\lambda\hat{k}_{,}\vec{a}_{2}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}=6\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-(\lambda+4)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}_{1}=-2\hat{i}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}| \\ & =-\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $(\vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}) \cdot \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=-6+1-\lambda+2\lambda+8=\lambda+3$ and $|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|=\sqrt{6}$ $\because \frac{|\lambda+3|}{\sqrt{6}}=2\sqrt{6}$ $\therefore \lambda=9, \because \lambda \ge 0$ $\therefore L:\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-9}{0}=\frac{z+9}{1}=k$ $\therefore \alpha=-2k+5,\beta=9,\gamma=k-9$ Here $k$ is real then $\alpha+2\gamma=-13 \ne 24$ . But all other are in terms of $k$ hence possible.
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-\lambda}{0}=\frac{z+\lambda}{1},\lambda \ge 0$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-4}{-1} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{1}=5\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}-\lambda\hat{k}_{,}\vec{a}_{2}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}=6\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-(\lambda+4)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}_{1}=-2\hat{i}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}| \\ & =-\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$(\vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}) \cdot \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=-6+1-\lambda+2\lambda+8=\lambda+3$

and $|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|=\sqrt{6}$

$\because \frac{|\lambda+3|}{\sqrt{6}}=2\sqrt{6}$

$\therefore \lambda=9, \because \lambda \ge 0$

$\therefore L:\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-9}{0}=\frac{z+9}{1}=k$

$\therefore \alpha=-2k+5,\beta=9,\gamma=k-9$

Here $k$ is real then

$\alpha+2\gamma=-13 \ne 24$ .

But all other are in terms of $k$ hence possible.

questions.question_text: Let the plane containing the line of intersection of the planes P 1 : $x+(\lambda+4)y+z=1$ and P 2 : $2x+y+z=2$ pass through the points (0, 1, 0) and (1, 0, 1). Then the distance of the point (2 $\lambda,\lambda,-\lambda$ ) from the plane P 2 is :
questions.question_html:
Let the plane containing the line of intersection of the planes

P1 : $x+(\lambda+4)y+z=1$ and

P2 : $2x+y+z=2$

pass through the points (0, 1, 0) and (1, 0, 1). Then the distance of

the point (2 $\lambda,\lambda,-\lambda$ ) from the plane P2 is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane passing through point of intersection of $P1$ and $P2$ $\begin{aligned} & P_{1}+kP_{2}=0 \\ \\ & (x+(\lambda+4)y+z-1)+k(2x+y+z-2)=0 \end{aligned}$ Passing through $(0,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$ $\begin{aligned} & (\lambda+4-1)+k(1-2)=0 \\ \\ & (\lambda+3)-k=0...(1) \end{aligned}$ Also passing $(1,0,1)$ $\begin{aligned} & (1+1-1)+k(2+1-2)=0 \\ \\ & 1+k=0 \\ \\ & k=-1 \end{aligned}$ put in (1) $\begin{aligned} & \lambda+3+1=0 \\ \\ & \lambda=-4 \end{aligned}$ Then point $(2\lambda,\lambda,-\lambda)$ $\begin{aligned} & (-8,-4,4) \\ \\ & d=|\frac{-16-4+4-2}{\sqrt{6}}| \\ \\ & d=\frac{18}{\sqrt{6}} \times \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}}=3\sqrt{6} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of plane passing through point of intersection of $P1$ and $P2$

$\begin{aligned} & P_{1}+kP_{2}=0 \\ \\ & (x+(\lambda+4)y+z-1)+k(2x+y+z-2)=0 \end{aligned}$

Passing through $(0,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$

$\begin{aligned} & (\lambda+4-1)+k(1-2)=0 \\ \\ & (\lambda+3)-k=0...(1) \end{aligned}$

Also passing $(1,0,1)$

$\begin{aligned} & (1+1-1)+k(2+1-2)=0 \\ \\ & 1+k=0 \\ \\ & k=-1 \end{aligned}$

put in (1)

$\begin{aligned} & \lambda+3+1=0 \\ \\ & \lambda=-4 \end{aligned}$

Then point $(2\lambda,\lambda,-\lambda)$

$\begin{aligned} & (-8,-4,4) \\ \\ & d=|\frac{-16-4+4-2}{\sqrt{6}}| \\ \\ & d=\frac{18}{\sqrt{6}} \times \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}}=3\sqrt{6} \end{aligned}$

$A(8,-1,-19)$ from the plane $P$ measured parallel to the line $\frac{x}{-3}=\frac{y-5}{4}=\frac{2-z}{-12}$

questions.explanation_text: Plane $P \equiv P_{1}+\lambda P_{2}=0$ $\begin{aligned} & (2x+y-z-3)+\lambda(5x-3y)+4z+9)=0 \\ \\ & (5\lambda+2)x+(1-3\lambda)y+(4\lambda-1)z+9\lambda-3=0 \\ \\ & \vec{n} \cdot \vec{b}=0\text{where}\vec{b}(2,4,5) \\ \\ & 2(5\lambda+2)+4(1-3\lambda)+5(4\lambda-1)=0 \\ \\ & \lambda=-\frac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$ Plane $7x+9y-10z-27=0$ Equation of line $AB$ is $\frac{x-8}{-3}=\frac{y+1}{4}=\frac{z+19}{12}=\lambda$ Let $B=(8-3\lambda,-1+4\lambda,-19+12\lambda)$ lies on plane $P$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 7(8-3\lambda)+9(4\lambda-1)-10(12\lambda-19)=27 \\ \\ & \lambda=2 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Point}B=(2,7,5) \\ \\ & AB=\sqrt{6^{2}+8^{2}+24^{2}}=26 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let a line $l$ pass through the origin and be perpendicular to the lines $l_{1}:\vec{r}=(\hat{ı}-11\hat{ȷ}-7\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{ȷ}+3\hat{k}),\lambda \in ℝ$ and $l_{2}:\vec{r}=(-\hat{ı}+\hat{k})+\mu(2\hat{ı}+2\hat{ȷ}+\hat{k}),\mu \in ℝ$ . If $P$ is the point of intersection of $l$ and $l_{1}$ , and $Q(∝,\beta,\gamma)$ is the foot of perpendicular from P on $l_{2}$ , then $9(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to _____________.
questions.question_html:
Let a line $l$ pass through the origin and be perpendicular to the lines

$l_{1}:\vec{r}=(\hat{ı}-11\hat{ȷ}-7\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{ȷ}+3\hat{k}),\lambda \in ℝ$ and

$l_{2}:\vec{r}=(-\hat{ı}+\hat{k})+\mu(2\hat{ı}+2\hat{ȷ}+\hat{k}),\mu \in ℝ$ .

If $P$ is the point of intersection of $l$ and $l_{1}$ , and $Q(∝,\beta,\gamma)$ is the foot of perpendicular from P on $l_{2}$ , then $9(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to _____________.
questions.explanation_text: We have, $l_{1}:\vec{r}=(\hat{ı}-11\hat{ȷ}-7\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{ȷ}+3\hat{k}),\lambda \in ℝ$ and $l_{2}:\vec{r}=(-\hat{ı}+\hat{k})+\mu(2\hat{ı}+2\hat{ȷ}+\hat{k}),\mu \in ℝ$ . Let direction ratio of line $l$ be $a,b$ and $c$ Equation of line $l$ $\begin{aligned} \vec{r} & =(0\hat{i}+0\hat{j}+0\hat{k})+\delta(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =\delta(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$ As, line $l$ is perpendicular to $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ , $a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-4\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ Equation of line $l:\vec{r}=\delta(-4\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$ As, $P$ is the intersecting point of $l$ and $l_{1}$ $-4\delta=1+\lambda,5\delta=-11+2\lambda,-2\delta=-7+3\lambda$ After solving the above three equation, we get $\delta=-1\text{and}\lambda=3$ $\therefore$ Co-ordinate of point $P$ is $(4,-5,2)$ . $Q$ is a point on line $l_{2}$ Let co-ordinate of $Q$ be $(-1+2\mu,2\mu,1+\mu)$ $\begin{aligned} \vec{PQ}=(-5+2\mu)\hat{i}+(2\mu+5)\hat{j}+(\mu-1)\hat{k} \\ \\ \vec{PQ} \cdot (2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=0[ \because \vec{PQ}⟂l_{2}] \\ \\ 2(-5+2\mu)+2(2\mu+5)+\mu-1=0 \\ \\ 9\mu-1=0 \Rightarrow \mu=\frac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \alpha=-1+\frac{2}{9}=\frac{-7}{9},\beta=2 \times \frac{1}{9}=\frac{2}{9},r=1+\frac{1}{9}=\frac{10}{9} \\ \\ & \text{Hence,}9(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=9(-\frac{7}{9}+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{10}{9})=5 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
We have,

$l_{1}:\vec{r}=(\hat{ı}-11\hat{ȷ}-7\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{ȷ}+3\hat{k}),\lambda \in ℝ$ and

$l_{2}:\vec{r}=(-\hat{ı}+\hat{k})+\mu(2\hat{ı}+2\hat{ȷ}+\hat{k}),\mu \in ℝ$ .

Let direction ratio of line $l$ be $a,b$ and $c$ Equation of line $l$

$\begin{aligned} \vec{r} & =(0\hat{i}+0\hat{j}+0\hat{k})+\delta(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =\delta(a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$

As, line $l$ is perpendicular to $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ ,

$a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-4\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ Equation of line $l:\vec{r}=\delta(-4\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$

As, $P$ is the intersecting point of $l$ and $l_{1}$

$-4\delta=1+\lambda,5\delta=-11+2\lambda,-2\delta=-7+3\lambda$

After solving the above three equation, we get

$\delta=-1\text{and}\lambda=3$

$\therefore$ Co-ordinate of point $P$ is $(4,-5,2)$ .

$Q$ is a point on line $l_{2}$

Let co-ordinate of $Q$ be $(-1+2\mu,2\mu,1+\mu)$

$\begin{aligned} \vec{PQ}=(-5+2\mu)\hat{i}+(2\mu+5)\hat{j}+(\mu-1)\hat{k} \\ \\ \vec{PQ} \cdot (2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=0[ \because \vec{PQ}⟂l_{2}] \\ \\ 2(-5+2\mu)+2(2\mu+5)+\mu-1=0 \\ \\ 9\mu-1=0 \Rightarrow \mu=\frac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \alpha=-1+\frac{2}{9}=\frac{-7}{9},\beta=2 \times \frac{1}{9}=\frac{2}{9},r=1+\frac{1}{9}=\frac{10}{9} \\ \\ & \text{Hence,}9(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=9(-\frac{7}{9}+\frac{2}{9}+\frac{10}{9})=5 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If the lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{2-y}{-3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{x-4}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{\beta}$ intersect, then the magnitude of the minimum value of $8\alpha\beta$ is _____________.
questions.question_html: If the lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{2-y}{-3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{x-4}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{\beta}$ intersect, then the magnitude of the minimum value of $8\alpha\beta$ is _____________.
questions.explanation_text: Given, lines $\begin{aligned} & \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{2-y}{-3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha}=\lambda.........(i) \end{aligned}$ Any point on the line (i) $x=2\lambda+1,y=3\lambda+2,z=\alpha\lambda+3$ and line $\frac{x-4}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{\beta}=\mu$ ............(ii) Any point on line (ii) $\Rightarrow x=5\mu+4,y=2\mu+1,z=\beta\mu$ Since, given lines intersects $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 2\lambda+1=5\mu+4..........(iii) \\ \\ & 3\lambda+2=2\mu+1............(iv) \\ \\ & \text{and}\alpha\lambda+3=\beta\mu..........(iv) \end{aligned}$ On solving (iii) and (iv), we get $\lambda=-1,\mu=-1$ On putting value of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ in (v), we get $\begin{aligned} & \alpha(-1)+3=-\beta \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=\beta+3 \end{aligned}$ Now, $\begin{aligned} & 8\alpha\beta=8(\beta+3)(\beta) \\ \\ & =8(\beta^{2}+3\beta) \\ \\ & =8(\beta^{2}+3\beta+\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{4}) \\ \\ & =8{(\beta+\frac{3}{2})^{2}-\frac{9}{4}} \end{aligned}$ $=8(\beta+\frac{3}{2})^{2}-18$ Here, minimum value $=-18$ $\therefore$ Magnitude of the minimum value of $8\alpha\beta$ is 18 .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, lines

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{2-y}{-3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{\alpha}=\lambda.........(i) \end{aligned}$

Any point on the line (i)

$x=2\lambda+1,y=3\lambda+2,z=\alpha\lambda+3$

and line $\frac{x-4}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{\beta}=\mu$ ............(ii)

Any point on line (ii)

$\Rightarrow x=5\mu+4,y=2\mu+1,z=\beta\mu$

Since, given lines intersects

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore 2\lambda+1=5\mu+4..........(iii) \\ \\ & 3\lambda+2=2\mu+1............(iv) \\ \\ & \text{and}\alpha\lambda+3=\beta\mu..........(iv) \end{aligned}$

On solving (iii) and (iv), we get

$\lambda=-1,\mu=-1$

On putting value of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ in (v), we get

$\begin{aligned} & \alpha(-1)+3=-\beta \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=\beta+3 \end{aligned}$

Now,

$\begin{aligned} & 8\alpha\beta=8(\beta+3)(\beta) \\ \\ & =8(\beta^{2}+3\beta) \\ \\ & =8(\beta^{2}+3\beta+\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{4}) \\ \\ & =8{(\beta+\frac{3}{2})^{2}-\frac{9}{4}} \end{aligned}$

$=8(\beta+\frac{3}{2})^{2}-18$

Here, minimum value $=-18$

$\therefore$ Magnitude of the minimum value of $8\alpha\beta$ is 18 .

questions.question_text: Let the line $L:\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}$ intersect the plane $2x+y+3z=16$ at the point $P$ . Let the point $Q$ be the foot of perpendicular from the point $R(1,-1,-3)$ on the line $L$ . If $\alpha$ is the area of triangle $PQR$ , then $\alpha^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: Let the line $L:\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}$ intersect the plane $2x+y+3z=16$ at the point $P$ . Let the point $Q$ be the foot of perpendicular from the point $R(1,-1,-3)$ on the line $L$ . If $\alpha$ is the area of triangle $PQR$ , then $\alpha^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_html:
$L:\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}=r$ (say)

Let $P \equiv (2r_{1}+1,-r_{1},r_{1}+3)$

$P$ lies on $2x+y+3z=16$

$\therefore 2(2r_{1}+1)+(-r_{1}-1)+3(r_{1}+3)=16$

$r_{1}=1$

$P \equiv (3,-2,4)$

$R \equiv (1,-1,-3)$

Let $Q \equiv (2r_{2}+1,-r_{2}-1,r_{2}+3)$

$DR$ s of $QR \equiv (2r_{2}-r_{2}r_{2}+6)$

DRs of $L \equiv (2,-1,1)$

$QR⟂L \Rightarrow 4r_{2}+r_{2}+r_{2}+6=0$

$r_{2}=-1$

$Q \equiv (-1,0,2)$

$\vec{QP} \times \vec{RP}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 7 \end{aligned}|=-12\hat{i}-24\hat{j}+0\hat{k}$

$\alpha=[PQR]=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{QP} \times \vec{RP}|=\frac{1}{2} \times 12\sqrt{5}$

$=6\sqrt{5}$

$\alpha^{2}=180$

questions.question_text: If $\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}$ are two values of $\lambda$ such that the angle between the planes $P_{1}:\vec{r}(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k})=7$ and $P_{2}:\vec{r} \cdot (\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k})=9$ is $sin^{-1}(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5})$ , then the square of the length of perpendicular from the point $(38\lambda_{1},10\lambda_{2},2)$ to the plane $P_{1}$ is ______________.
questions.question_html: If $\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}$ are two values of $\lambda$ such that the angle between the planes $P_{1}:\vec{r}(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k})=7$ and $P_{2}:\vec{r} \cdot (\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k})=9$ is $sin^{-1}(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5})$ , then the square of the length of perpendicular from the point $(38\lambda_{1},10\lambda_{2},2)$ to the plane $P_{1}$ is ______________.
questions.explanation_text: $P_{1}:\vec{r}.(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k})=7$ $P_{2}:\vec{r}.(\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k})=9$ Let angle between P 1 and P 2 is $\theta$ Then $cos\theta=\frac{3\lambda-5-3}{\sqrt{35}\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+10}}$ But $sin\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{(3\lambda-8)^{2}}{35(\lambda^{2}+10)}=1-\frac{24}{25}$ $\Rightarrow 5(9\lambda^{2}+64-48\lambda)=7\lambda^{2}+70$ $\Rightarrow 38\lambda^{2}-240\lambda+250=0$ $\Rightarrow 19\lambda^{2}-120\lambda+125=0$ $\Rightarrow (19\lambda-25)(\lambda-5)=0$ $\therefore$ $\lambda_{1}=\frac{25}{19},\lambda_{2}=5$ So, point (50, 50, 2) $\therefore$ $d=\frac{|150-250+2-7|}{\sqrt{35}}=315$
questions.explanation_html:
$P_{1}:\vec{r}.(3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k})=7$

$P_{2}:\vec{r}.(\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k})=9$

Let angle between P1 and P2 is $\theta$

Then $cos\theta=\frac{3\lambda-5-3}{\sqrt{35}\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+10}}$

But $sin\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{(3\lambda-8)^{2}}{35(\lambda^{2}+10)}=1-\frac{24}{25}$

$\Rightarrow 5(9\lambda^{2}+64-48\lambda)=7\lambda^{2}+70$

$\Rightarrow 38\lambda^{2}-240\lambda+250=0$

$\Rightarrow 19\lambda^{2}-120\lambda+125=0$

$\Rightarrow (19\lambda-25)(\lambda-5)=0$

$\therefore$ $\lambda_{1}=\frac{25}{19},\lambda_{2}=5$

So, point (50, 50, 2)

$\therefore$ $d=\frac{|150-250+2-7|}{\sqrt{35}}=315$

questions.question_html: Let the equation of the plane passing through the line $x-2y-z-5=0=x+y+3z-5$ and parallel to the line $x+y+2z-7=0=2x+3y+z-2$ be $ax+by+cz=65$ . Then the distance of the point (a, b, c) from the plane $2x+2y-z+16=0$ is ____________.
questions.explanation_text: Let the equation of the plane is $(x-2y-z-5)+\lambda(x+y+3z-5)=0$ $\because$ it's parallel to the line $x+y+2z-7=0=2x+3y+z-2$ So, vector along the line $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $=-5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $\because$ Plane is parallel to line $\therefore -5(1+\lambda)+3(-2+\lambda)+1(-1+3\lambda)=0$ $\lambda=12$ So, by (i) $13x+10y+35z=65$ $\therefore a=13,b=10,c=35$ and $d=\frac{26+20-35+16}{\sqrt{9}}=9$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the equation of the plane is

$(x-2y-z-5)+\lambda(x+y+3z-5)=0$

$\because$ it's parallel to the line

$x+y+2z-7=0=2x+3y+z-2$

So, vector along the line $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$=-5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$\because$ Plane is parallel to line

$\therefore -5(1+\lambda)+3(-2+\lambda)+1(-1+3\lambda)=0$

$\lambda=12$

So, by (i)

$13x+10y+35z=65$

$\therefore a=13,b=10,c=35$ and $d=\frac{26+20-35+16}{\sqrt{9}}=9$

questions.question_html: If the foot of the perpendicular from the point $A(-1,4,3)$ on the plane $P:2x+my+nz=4$ , is $(-2,\frac{7}{2},\frac{3}{2})$ , then the distance of the point A from the plane P, measured parallel to a line with direction ratios $3,-1,-4$ , is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $(-2,\frac{7}{2},\frac{3}{2})$ satisfies the plane $P:2x+my+nz=4$ $-4+\frac{7m}{2}+\frac{3n}{2}=4 \Rightarrow 7m+3n=16$ ...... (i) Line joining $A(-1,4,3)$ and $(-2,\frac{7}{2},\frac{3}{2})$ is perpendicular to $P:2x+my+nz=4$ $\frac{1}{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{m}=\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{n} \Rightarrow m=1$ & $n=3$ Plane $P:2x+y+3z=4$ Distance of P from $A(-1,4,3)$ parallel to the line $\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{y-4}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{-4}:L$ for point of intersection of P & L $2(3r-1)+(-r+4)+3(-4r+3)=4 \Rightarrow r=1$ Point of intersection : $(2,3,-1)$ Required distance $=\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{26}$

$-4+\frac{7m}{2}+\frac{3n}{2}=4 \Rightarrow 7m+3n=16$ ...... (i)

for point of intersection of P & L

questions.question_text: If the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point $P(a,4,2)$ , a $>0$ on the line $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z-1}{-1}$ is $2\sqrt{6}$ units and $Q(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})$ is the image of the point P in this line, then $a+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point $P(a,4,2)$ , a $>0$ on the line $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z-1}{-1}$ is $2\sqrt{6}$ units and $Q(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})$ is the image of the point P in this line, then $a+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\because$ PR is perpendicular to given line, so $2(2\lambda-1-a)+3(3\lambda-1)-1(-\lambda-1)=0$ $\Rightarrow a=7\lambda-2$ Now, $\because$ $PR=2\sqrt{6}$ $\Rightarrow (-5\lambda+1)^{2}+(3\lambda-1)^{2}+(\lambda+1)^{2}=24$ $\Rightarrow 5\lambda^{2}-2\lambda-3=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=1$ or $-\frac{3}{5}$ $\because$ $a>0$ so $\lambda=1$ and $a=5$ Now $\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}=2$ (Sum of co-ordinate of R) $-$ (Sum of coordinates of P) $=2(7)-11=3$ $a+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}=5+3=8$
questions.explanation_html:
$\because$ PR is perpendicular to given line, so

$2(2\lambda-1-a)+3(3\lambda-1)-1(-\lambda-1)=0$

$\Rightarrow a=7\lambda-2$

Now,

$\because$ $PR=2\sqrt{6}$

$\Rightarrow (-5\lambda+1)^{2}+(3\lambda-1)^{2}+(\lambda+1)^{2}=24$

$\Rightarrow 5\lambda^{2}-2\lambda-3=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=1$ or $-\frac{3}{5}$

$\because$ $a>0$ so $\lambda=1$ and $a=5$

Now $\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}=2$ (Sum of co-ordinate of R) $-$ (Sum of coordinates of P)

$=2(7)-11=3$

$a+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}=5+3=8$

questions.question_html: The length of the perpendicular from the point $(1,-2,5)$ on the line passing through $(1,2,4)$ and parallel to the line $x+y-z=0=x-2y+3z-5$ is :
questions.explanation_text: The line $x+y-z=0=x-2y+3z-5$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{aligned}|=(1,4,-3)$ Equation of the line through $P(1,2,4)$ and parallel to $\vec{b}$ $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-4}{-3}$ Let $N \equiv (\lambda+1,-4\lambda+2,-3\lambda+4)$ $\vec{QN}=(\lambda,-4\lambda+4,-3\lambda-1)$ $\vec{QN}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow (\lambda,-4\lambda+4,-3\lambda-1).(1,4,-3)=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ Hence $\vec{QN}=(\frac{1}{2},2,\frac{-5}{2})$ and $|\vec{QN}|=\sqrt{\frac{21}{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
The line $x+y-z=0=x-2y+3z-5$ is parallel to the vector

$\vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \end{aligned}|=(1,4,-3)$

Equation of the line through $P(1,2,4)$ and parallel to $\vec{b}$

$\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-4}{-3}$

$\vec{QN}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$

questions.question_html: The distance of the point (3, 2, $-$ 1) from the plane $3x-y+4z+1=0$ along the line $\frac{2-x}{2}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Line PQ is parallel to line $\frac{2-x}{2}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ $\therefore$ DR of PQ = DR of line = < $-$ 2, 2, 1> $\therefore$ Equation of line PQ passing through P(3, 2, $-$ 1) and DR = < $-$ 2, 2, 1> is $\frac{x-3}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ Any General point on line PQ = (x 1 , y 1 , z 1 ) $\therefore$ $\frac{x_{1}-3}{-2}=\frac{y_{1}-2}{2}=\frac{z_{1}+1}{1}=\lambda$ $\Rightarrow x_{1}=-2\lambda+3$ $y_{1}=2\lambda+2$ $z_{1}=\lambda-1$ $\therefore$ Point Q = ( $-$ 2 $\lambda$ + 3, 2 $\lambda$ + 2, $\lambda$ $-$ 1) Point Q lies on the plane $3x-y+4z+1=0$ . So point Q satisfy the equation. $3(-2\lambda+3)-(2\lambda+2)+4(\lambda-1)+1=0$ $\Rightarrow -6\lambda+9-2\lambda-2+4\lambda-4+1=0$ $\Rightarrow -4\lambda+4=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=1$ $\therefore$ Point Q = ( $-$ 2 $\times$ 1 + 3, 2 $\times$ 1 + 2, 1 $-$ 1) = (1, 4, 0) $\therefore$ Distance of the point P(3, 2, $-$ 1) from the plane = Length of PQ $=\sqrt{(3-1)^{2}+(2-4)^{2}+(-1-0)^{2}}$ $=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}$ $=\sqrt{4+4+1}$ $=\sqrt{9}$ $=3$
questions.explanation_html:
Line PQ is parallel to line $\frac{2-x}{2}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$

$\therefore$ DR of PQ = DR of line = < $-$ 2, 2, 1>

$\therefore$ Equation of line PQ passing through P(3, 2, $-$ 1) and DR = < $-$ 2, 2, 1> is

$\frac{x-3}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}$

Any General point on line PQ = (x1, y1, z1)

$\therefore$ $\frac{x_{1}-3}{-2}=\frac{y_{1}-2}{2}=\frac{z_{1}+1}{1}=\lambda$

$\Rightarrow x_{1}=-2\lambda+3$

$y_{1}=2\lambda+2$

$z_{1}=\lambda-1$

$\therefore$ Point Q = ( $-$ 2 $\lambda$ + 3, 2 $\lambda$ + 2, $\lambda$ $-$ 1)

Point Q lies on the plane $3x-y+4z+1=0$ . So point Q satisfy the equation.

$3(-2\lambda+3)-(2\lambda+2)+4(\lambda-1)+1=0$

$\Rightarrow -6\lambda+9-2\lambda-2+4\lambda-4+1=0$

$\Rightarrow -4\lambda+4=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=1$

$\therefore$ Point Q = ( $-$ 2 $\times$ 1 + 3, 2 $\times$ 1 + 2, 1 $-$ 1)

= (1, 4, 0)

$\therefore$ Distance of the point P(3, 2, $-$ 1) from the plane = Length of PQ

$=\sqrt{(3-1)^{2}+(2-4)^{2}+(-1-0)^{2}}$

$=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}$

$=\sqrt{4+4+1}$

$=\sqrt{9}$

$=3$

questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane containing the line $4ax-y+5z-7a=0=2x-5y-z-3$ can be written as $4ax-y+5z-7a+\lambda(2x-5y-z-3)=0$ $(4a+2\lambda)x-(1+5\lambda)y+(5-\lambda)z-(7z+3\lambda)=0$ Which is coplanar with the line $\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z}{1}$ $4(4a+2\lambda)+(1+5\lambda)-(7a+3\lambda)=0$ $9a+10\lambda+1=0$ ..... (1) $(4a+2\lambda)1+(1+5\lambda)2+5-\lambda=0$ $4a+11\lambda+7=0$ ...... (2) $a=1,\lambda=-1$ Equation of plane is $x+2y+3z-2=0$ Intersection with the line $\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{-4}$ $(7t+3)+2(-t+2)+3(-4t+3)-2=0$ $-7t+14=0$ $t=2$ So, the required point is $(17,0,-5)$ $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=12$
questions.explanation_html:

$4ax-y+5z-7a+\lambda(2x-5y-z-3)=0$

$(4a+2\lambda)x-(1+5\lambda)y+(5-\lambda)z-(7z+3\lambda)=0$

Which is coplanar with the line

$\frac{x-4}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z}{1}$

$4(4a+2\lambda)+(1+5\lambda)-(7a+3\lambda)=0$

$9a+10\lambda+1=0$ ..... (1)

$(4a+2\lambda)1+(1+5\lambda)2+5-\lambda=0$

$4a+11\lambda+7=0$ ...... (2)

$a=1,\lambda=-1$

Equation of plane is $x+2y+3z-2=0$

Intersection with the line

$\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{-4}$

$(7t+3)+2(-t+2)+3(-4t+3)-2=0$

$-7t+14=0$

$t=2$

So, the required point is $(17,0,-5)$

$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=12$

questions.explanation_text: The point dividing PQ in the ratio 1 : 3 will be mid-point of P & foot of perpendicular from P on the line. $\therefore$ Let a point on line be $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{3}=\lambda$ $\Rightarrow P^{'}(3\lambda+6,2\lambda+1,3\lambda+2)$ as P' is foot of perpendicular $(3\lambda+5)3+(2\lambda-1)2+(3\lambda-1)3=0$ $\Rightarrow 22\lambda+15-2-3=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-5}{11}$ $\therefore$ $P^{'}(\frac{51}{11},\frac{1}{11},\frac{7}{11})$ Mid-point of $PP^{'} \equiv (\frac{\frac{51}{11}+1}{2},\frac{\frac{1}{11}+2}{2},\frac{\frac{7}{11}+3}{2})$ $\equiv (\frac{62}{22},\frac{23}{22},\frac{40}{22}) \equiv (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ $\Rightarrow 22(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=62+23+40=125$

$\equiv (\frac{62}{22},\frac{23}{22},\frac{40}{22}) \equiv (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$

questions.question_html:
Let the lines

questions.explanation_text: $L_{1}:\frac{x-1}{\lambda}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-3}{2}$ , through a point $\vec{a}_{1} \equiv (1,2,3)$ parallel to $\vec{b}_{1} \equiv (\lambda,1,2)$ $L_{2}:\frac{x+26}{-2}=\frac{y+18}{3}=\frac{z+28}{\lambda}$ through a point $\vec{a}_{2}=(-26,-18,-28)$ parallel to $\vec{b}_{2}=(-2,3,1)$ If lines are coplanar then, $(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}).\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 27 & 20 & 31 \\ \lambda & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & \lambda \end{aligned}|=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=3$ Vector normal to the required plane $\vec{n}=\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}$ $\Rightarrow \vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & 3 \end{aligned}|=-3\hat{i}-13\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$ Equation of plane $\equiv ((x-1),(y-2),(z-3)).(-3,-13,11)=0$ $\Rightarrow 3x+13y-11z+4=0$ Checking the option gives (0, 4, 5) does not lie on the plane.
questions.explanation_html:

parallel to $\vec{b}_{1} \equiv (\lambda,1,2)$

$L_{2}:\frac{x+26}{-2}=\frac{y+18}{3}=\frac{z+28}{\lambda}$

through a point $\vec{a}_{2}=(-26,-18,-28)$

parallel to $\vec{b}_{2}=(-2,3,1)$

If lines are coplanar then, $(\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}).\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 27 & 20 & 31 \\ \lambda & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & \lambda \end{aligned}|=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=3$

Vector normal to the required plane $\vec{n}=\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}$

$\Rightarrow \vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & 3 \end{aligned}|=-3\hat{i}-13\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$

Equation of plane

$\equiv ((x-1),(y-2),(z-3)).(-3,-13,11)=0$

$\Rightarrow 3x+13y-11z+4=0$

Checking the option gives (0, 4, 5) does not lie on the plane.

questions.explanation_text: $P_{1}:ax+by+0z=3$ , normal vector : $\vec{n}_{1}=(a,b,0)$ $P_{2}:ax+by+cz=0$ , normal vector : $\vec{n}_{2}=(a,b,c)$ Vector parallel to the line of intersection $=\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}$ $\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}=(bc,-ac,0)$ Vector normal to $0.x+y-z+2=0$ is $\vec{n}_{3}=(0,1,-1)$ Angle between line and plane is 30 $^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow |\frac{0-ac+0}{\sqrt{b^{2}c^{2}+c^{2}a^{2}}\sqrt{2}}|=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow a^{2}=b^{2}$ Hence, $\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}=(ac,-ac,0)$ Direction ratios $=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},0)$
questions.explanation_html:
$P_{1}:ax+by+0z=3$ , normal vector : $\vec{n}_{1}=(a,b,0)$

$P_{2}:ax+by+cz=0$ , normal vector : $\vec{n}_{2}=(a,b,c)$

Vector parallel to the line of intersection $=\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}$

$\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}=(bc,-ac,0)$

Vector normal to $0.x+y-z+2=0$ is $\vec{n}_{3}=(0,1,-1)$

Angle between line and plane is 30 $^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow |\frac{0-ac+0}{\sqrt{b^{2}c^{2}+c^{2}a^{2}}\sqrt{2}}|=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow a^{2}=b^{2}$

Hence, $\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}=(ac,-ac,0)$

Direction ratios $=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},0)$

questions.question_text: A plane $E$ is perpendicular to the two planes $2x-2y+z=0$ and $x-y+2z=4$ , and passes through the point $P(1,-1,1)$ . If the distance of the plane $E$ from the point $Q(a,a,2)$ is $3\sqrt{2}$ , then $(PQ)^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: A plane $E$ is perpendicular to the two planes $2x-2y+z=0$ and $x-y+2z=4$ , and passes through the point $P(1,-1,1)$ . If the distance of the plane $E$ from the point $Q(a,a,2)$ is $3\sqrt{2}$ , then $(PQ)^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: First plane, $P_{1}=2x-2y+z=0$ , normal vector $\equiv \bar{n}_{1}=(2,-2,1)$ Second plane, $P_{2} \equiv x-y+2z=4$ , normal vector $\equiv \bar{n}_{2}=(1,-1,2)$ Plane perpendicular to P 1 and P 2 will have normal vector $\bar{n}_{3}$ Where $\bar{n}_{3}=(\bar{n}_{1} \times \bar{n}_{2})$ Hence, $\bar{n}_{3}=(-3,-3,0)$ Equation of plane E through $P(1,-1,1)$ and $\bar{n}_{3}$ as normal vector $(x-1,y+1,z-1).(-3,-3,0)=0$ $\Rightarrow x+y=0 \equiv E$ Distance of $PQ(a,a,2)$ from $E=|\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2}}|$ as given, $|\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2}}|=3\sqrt{2} \Rightarrow a= \pm 3$ Hence, $Q \equiv ( \pm 3, \pm 3,2)$ Distance $7Q=\sqrt{21} \Rightarrow (PQ)^{2}=21$
questions.explanation_html:
First plane, $P_{1}=2x-2y+z=0$ , normal vector $\equiv \bar{n}_{1}=(2,-2,1)$

Second plane, $P_{2} \equiv x-y+2z=4$ , normal vector $\equiv \bar{n}_{2}=(1,-1,2)$

Plane perpendicular to P1 and P2 will have normal vector $\bar{n}_{3}$

Where $\bar{n}_{3}=(\bar{n}_{1} \times \bar{n}_{2})$

Hence, $\bar{n}_{3}=(-3,-3,0)$

Equation of plane E through $P(1,-1,1)$ and $\bar{n}_{3}$ as normal vector

$(x-1,y+1,z-1).(-3,-3,0)=0$

$\Rightarrow x+y=0 \equiv E$

Distance of $PQ(a,a,2)$ from $E=|\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2}}|$

as given, $|\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2}}|=3\sqrt{2} \Rightarrow a= \pm 3$

Hence, $Q \equiv ( \pm 3, \pm 3,2)$

Distance $7Q=\sqrt{21} \Rightarrow (PQ)^{2}=21$

questions.question_html: Let $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z+3}{-1}$ lie on the plane $px-qy+z=5$ , for some p, q $\in$ R. The shortest distance of the plane from the origin is :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z+3}{-1}=\lambda$ $(3\lambda+2,-2\lambda-1,-\lambda-3)$ lies on plane $px-qy+z=5$ $p(3\lambda+2)-q(-2\lambda-1)+(-\lambda-3)=5$ $\lambda(3p+2q-1)+(2p+q-8)=0$ $3p+2q-1=0}p=15$ $2p+q-8=0}q=-22$ Equation of plane $15x+22y+z-5=0$ Shortest distance from origin $=\frac{|0+0+0-5|}{\sqrt{15^{2}+22^{2}+1}}$ $=\frac{5}{\sqrt{710}}$ $=\sqrt{\frac{5}{142}}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z+3}{-1}=\lambda$

$(3\lambda+2,-2\lambda-1,-\lambda-3)$ lies on plane $px-qy+z=5$

$p(3\lambda+2)-q(-2\lambda-1)+(-\lambda-3)=5$

$\lambda(3p+2q-1)+(2p+q-8)=0$

$3p+2q-1=0}p=15$

$2p+q-8=0}q=-22$

Equation of plane $15x+22y+z-5=0$

Shortest distance from origin $=\frac{|0+0+0-5|}{\sqrt{15^{2}+22^{2}+1}}$

$=\frac{5}{\sqrt{710}}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{5}{142}}$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ , $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ be three given vectors. Let $\vec{v}$ be a vector in the plane of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ whose projection on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ . If $\vec{v}.\hat{j}=7$ , then $\vec{v}.(\hat{i}+\hat{k})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{v}=\lambda_{1}\vec{a}+\lambda_{2}\vec{b}$ , where $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} \in R$ . $=(\lambda_{1}+2\lambda_{2})\hat{i}+(\lambda_{1}-3\lambda_{2})\hat{j}+(2\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})\hat{k}$ $\because$ Projection of $\vec{v}$ on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{\lambda_{1}+2\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}+3\lambda_{2}+2\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\therefore$ $\lambda_{1}+3\lambda_{2}=1$ ..... (i) and $\vec{v}.\hat{j}=7 \Rightarrow \lambda_{1}-3\lambda_{2}=7$ ... (ii) from equation (i) and (ii) $\lambda_{1}=4$ , $\lambda_{2}=-1$ $\therefore$ $\vec{v}=2\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{v}.(\hat{i}+\hat{k})=2+7$ $=9$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{v}=\lambda_{1}\vec{a}+\lambda_{2}\vec{b}$ , where $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} \in R$ .

$=(\lambda_{1}+2\lambda_{2})\hat{i}+(\lambda_{1}-3\lambda_{2})\hat{j}+(2\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})\hat{k}$

$\because$ Projection of $\vec{v}$ on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{\lambda_{1}+2\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}+3\lambda_{2}+2\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\therefore$ $\lambda_{1}+3\lambda_{2}=1$ ..... (i)

and $\vec{v}.\hat{j}=7 \Rightarrow \lambda_{1}-3\lambda_{2}=7$ ... (ii)

from equation (i) and (ii)

$\lambda_{1}=4$ , $\lambda_{2}=-1$

$\therefore$ $\vec{v}=2\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{v}.(\hat{i}+\hat{k})=2+7$

$=9$

questions.question_text: Let Q be the mirror image of the point P(1, 0, 1) with respect to the plane S : x + y + z = 5. If a line L passing through (1, $-$ 1, $-$ 1), parallel to the line PQ meets the plane S at R, then QR 2 is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let Q be the mirror image of the point P(1, 0, 1) with respect to the plane S : x + y + z = 5. If a line L passing through (1, $-$ 1, $-$ 1), parallel to the line PQ meets the plane S at R, then QR2 is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: As L is parallel to PQ d.r.s of S is <1, 1, 1> $\therefore$ $L \equiv \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z+1}{1}$ Point of intersection of L and S be $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow (\lambda+1)+(\lambda-1)+(\lambda-1)=S$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=2$ $\therefore$ $R \equiv (3,1,1)$ Let $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\alpha-1}{1}=\frac{\beta}{1}=\frac{\gamma-1}{1}=\frac{-2(-3)}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=3,\beta=2,\gamma=3$ $\Rightarrow Q \equiv (3,2,3)$ $(QR)^{2}=0^{2}+(1)^{2}+(2)^{2}=5$
questions.explanation_html:
As L is parallel to PQ d.r.s of S is <1, 1, 1>

$\therefore$ $L \equiv \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z+1}{1}$

Point of intersection of L and S be $\lambda$

$\Rightarrow (\lambda+1)+(\lambda-1)+(\lambda-1)=S$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=2$

$\therefore$ $R \equiv (3,1,1)$

Let $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$

$\Rightarrow \frac{\alpha-1}{1}=\frac{\beta}{1}=\frac{\gamma-1}{1}=\frac{-2(-3)}{3}$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=3,\beta=2,\gamma=3$

$\Rightarrow Q \equiv (3,2,3)$

$(QR)^{2}=0^{2}+(1)^{2}+(2)^{2}=5$

questions.question_text: The largest value of $a$ , for which the perpendicular distance of the plane containing the lines $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+a\hat{j}-\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j})+\mu(-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-a\hat{k})$ from the point $(2,1,4)$ is $\sqrt{3}$ , is _________.
questions.question_html: The largest value of $a$ , for which the perpendicular distance of the plane containing the lines $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j})+\lambda(\hat{i}+a\hat{j}-\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j})+\mu(-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-a\hat{k})$ from the point $(2,1,4)$ is $\sqrt{3}$ , is _________.
questions.explanation_text: Normal to plane $=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & a & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -a \end{aligned}|$ $=\hat{i}(1-a^{2})-\hat{j}(-a-1)+\hat{k}(1+a)$ $=(1-a)\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ Plane $(1-a)(x-1)+(y-1)+z=0$ Distance from (2, 1, 4) is $\sqrt{3}$ i.e. $\Rightarrow |\frac{(1-a)+0+4}{\sqrt{(1-a)^{2}+1+1}}|=\sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow 25+a^{2}-10a=3a^{2}-6a+9$ $\Rightarrow 2a^{2}+4a-16=0$ $\Rightarrow a^{2}+2a-8=0$ $a=2$ or $-4$ $\therefore$ $a_{max}=2$
questions.explanation_html:
Normal to plane $=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & a & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -a \end{aligned}|$

$=\hat{i}(1-a^{2})-\hat{j}(-a-1)+\hat{k}(1+a)$

$=(1-a)\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ Plane $(1-a)(x-1)+(y-1)+z=0$

Distance from (2, 1, 4) is $\sqrt{3}$ i.e.

$\Rightarrow |\frac{(1-a)+0+4}{\sqrt{(1-a)^{2}+1+1}}|=\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow 25+a^{2}-10a=3a^{2}-6a+9$

$\Rightarrow 2a^{2}+4a-16=0$

$\Rightarrow a^{2}+2a-8=0$

$a=2$ or $-4$

$\therefore$ $a_{max}=2$

questions.question_text: Consider a triangle ABC whose vertices are A(0, $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ ), B( $\alpha$ , 0, $\alpha$ ) and C( $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ , 0), $\alpha$ > 0. Let D be a point moving on the line x + z $-$ 3 = 0 = y and G be the centroid of $\Delta$ ABC. If the minimum length of GD is $\sqrt{\frac{57}{2}}$ , then $\alpha$ is equal to ____________.
questions.question_html: Consider a triangle ABC whose vertices are A(0, $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ ), B( $\alpha$ , 0, $\alpha$ ) and C( $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ , 0), $\alpha$ > 0. Let D be a point moving on the line x + z $-$ 3 = 0 = y and G be the centroid of $\Delta$ ABC. If the minimum length of GD is $\sqrt{\frac{57}{2}}$ , then $\alpha$ is equal to ____________.
questions.explanation_text: Given, G is the centroid of $\Delta$ ABC $\therefore$ $G=(\frac{0+\alpha+\alpha}{3},\frac{\alpha+0+\alpha}{3},\frac{\alpha+\alpha+0}{3})$ $=(\frac{2\alpha}{3},\frac{2\alpha}{3},\frac{2\alpha}{3})$ Also given, D is a point moving on the line $x+z-3=0=y$ Let $D=(ℎ,0,k)$ $x+z-3=0 \Rightarrow ℎ+k-3=0 \Rightarrow ℎ=3-k$ $\therefore$ $D=(3-k,0,k)$ Now, length of $GD=d$ $=\sqrt{(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow d^{2}=(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)^{2}$ Differentiating both side with respect to k, we get $2dd^{'}=2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)+0+2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k) \times (-1)$ For maximum or minimum value of k, $d^{'}=0$ $\therefore$ $0=2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)-2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)$ $\Rightarrow 2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)=2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)$ $\Rightarrow -3+k=-k$ $\Rightarrow k=\frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore$ $GD^{2}=(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+\frac{3}{2})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-\frac{3}{2})^{2}=\frac{57}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{(4\alpha-9)^{2}}{36}+\frac{16\alpha^{2}}{36}+\frac{(4\alpha-9)^{2}}{36}=\frac{57}{2}$ $\Rightarrow (4\alpha-9)^{2}+16\alpha^{2}+(4\alpha-9)^{2}=57 \times 18$ $\Rightarrow 16\alpha^{2}-72\alpha+81+16\alpha^{2}+16\alpha^{2}-72\alpha+81=57 \times 18$ $\Rightarrow 48\alpha^{2}-144\alpha+162=1026$ $\Rightarrow 24\alpha^{2}-72\alpha+81-513=0$ $\Rightarrow 24\alpha^{2}-72\alpha-432=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-3\alpha-18=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-6\alpha+3\alpha-18=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha(\alpha-6)+3(\alpha-6)=0$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha-6)(\alpha+3)=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=6,-3$ Given, $\alpha>0$ $\therefore$ Possible value of $\alpha=6$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, G is the centroid of $\Delta$ ABC

$\therefore$ $G=(\frac{0+\alpha+\alpha}{3},\frac{\alpha+0+\alpha}{3},\frac{\alpha+\alpha+0}{3})$

$=(\frac{2\alpha}{3},\frac{2\alpha}{3},\frac{2\alpha}{3})$

Also given, D is a point moving on the line $x+z-3=0=y$

Let $D=(ℎ,0,k)$

$x+z-3=0 \Rightarrow ℎ+k-3=0 \Rightarrow ℎ=3-k$

$\therefore$ $D=(3-k,0,k)$

Now, length of $GD=d$

$=\sqrt{(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow d^{2}=(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)^{2}$

Differentiating both side with respect to k, we get

$2dd^{'}=2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)+0+2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k) \times (-1)$

For maximum or minimum value of k, $d^{'}=0$

$\therefore$ $0=2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)-2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)$

$\Rightarrow 2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+k)=2(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-k)$

$\Rightarrow -3+k=-k$

$\Rightarrow k=\frac{3}{2}$

$\therefore$ $GD^{2}=(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-3+\frac{3}{2})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3})^{2}+(\frac{2\alpha}{3}-\frac{3}{2})^{2}=\frac{57}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{(4\alpha-9)^{2}}{36}+\frac{16\alpha^{2}}{36}+\frac{(4\alpha-9)^{2}}{36}=\frac{57}{2}$

$\Rightarrow (4\alpha-9)^{2}+16\alpha^{2}+(4\alpha-9)^{2}=57 \times 18$

$\Rightarrow 16\alpha^{2}-72\alpha+81+16\alpha^{2}+16\alpha^{2}-72\alpha+81=57 \times 18$

$\Rightarrow 48\alpha^{2}-144\alpha+162=1026$

$\Rightarrow 24\alpha^{2}-72\alpha+81-513=0$

$\Rightarrow 24\alpha^{2}-72\alpha-432=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-3\alpha-18=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-6\alpha+3\alpha-18=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha(\alpha-6)+3(\alpha-6)=0$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha-6)(\alpha+3)=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=6,-3$

Given, $\alpha>0$

$\therefore$ Possible value of $\alpha=6$ .

questions.question_html:
If the shortest distance between the lines

$\vec{r}=(-\hat{i}+3\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}-a\hat{j})$

and $\vec{r}=(-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is $\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$ , then the integral value of a is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -a & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-a\hat{i}-\hat{j}+(a-1)\hat{k}$ $\vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ Shortest distance $=|\frac{(\vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}) \cdot (\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2})}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}|$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{2(a-1)}{\sqrt{a^{2}+1+(a-1)^{2}}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6(a^{2}-2a+1)=2a^{2}-2a+2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (a-2)(2a-1)=0 \Rightarrow a=2\text{because}a \in z. \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: If the plane $P$ passes through the intersection of two mutually perpendicular planes $2x+ky-5z=1$ and $3kx-ky+z=5,k<3$ and intercepts a unit length on positive $x$ -axis, then the intercept made by the plane $P$ on the $y$ -axis is :
questions.explanation_text: $P_{1}:2x+ky-5z=1$ $P_{2}:3kx-ky+z=5$ $\because$ $P_{1}\perpP_{2} \Rightarrow 6k-k^{2}+5=0$ $\Rightarrow k=1,5$ $\because$ $k<3$ $\therefore$ $k=1$ $P_{1}:2x+y-5z=1$ $P_{2}:3x-y+z=5$ $P:(2x+y-5z-1)+\lambda(3x-y+z-5)=0$ Positive x-axis intercept = 1 $\Rightarrow \frac{1+5\lambda}{2+3\lambda}=1$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ $P:7x+y-4z=7$ y intercept = 7.
questions.explanation_html:
$P_{1}:2x+ky-5z=1$

$\because$ $P_{1}\perpP_{2} \Rightarrow 6k-k^{2}+5=0$

$\Rightarrow k=1,5$

$\because$ $k<3$

$\therefore$ $k=1$

$P_{1}:2x+y-5z=1$

$P_{2}:3x-y+z=5$

Positive x-axis intercept = 1

$\Rightarrow \frac{1+5\lambda}{2+3\lambda}=1$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$ $P:7x+y-4z=7$

y intercept = 7.

questions.question_html: Let Q be the mirror image of the point P(1, 2, 1) with respect to the plane x + 2y + 2z = 16. Let T be a plane passing through the point Q and contains the line $\vec{r}=-\hat{k}+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}),\lambda \in R$ . Then, which of the following points lies on T?
questions.explanation_text: $P(1,2,1)$ image in plane $x+2y+2z=16$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-1}{2}=\frac{-2(1+2 \times 2+2 \times 1-16)}{1^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}} \\ \\ & \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-1}{2}=2 \\ \\ & Q(3,6,5) \\ \\ & \vec{r}=-\hat{k}+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$ $AQ=3\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} & =3(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \\ \\ & \vec{n}=(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \\ \\ & |\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =2\hat{i}-0\hat{j}-\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Equation of plane $\equiv 2(x-0)+0(y-0)-1(z+1)$ $=0$ $2x-z=1$ Point lying on plane from the option is $(1,2,1)$ i.e., option (B)

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-1}{2}=\frac{-2(1+2 \times 2+2 \times 1-16)}{1^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}} \\ \\ & \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-1}{2}=2 \\ \\ & Q(3,6,5) \\ \\ & \vec{r}=-\hat{k}+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$


$AQ=3\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$

Equation of plane $\equiv 2(x-0)+0(y-0)-1(z+1)$ $=0$

$2x-z=1$

Point lying on plane from the option is $(1,2,1)$ i.e., option (B)

questions.explanation_text: Family of Plane's equation can be given by $(5+8\lambda)x+(8-7\lambda)y+(13+\lambda)z-(29+20\lambda)=0$ P 1 passes through (2, 1, 3) $\Rightarrow (10+16\lambda)+(8-7\lambda)+(39+3\lambda)-(29+20\lambda)=0$ $\Rightarrow -8\lambda+28=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{7}{2}$ d.r, s of normal to P 1 $⟨33,\frac{-33}{2},\frac{33}{2}⟩$ or $⟨1,-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩$ P 2 passes through (0, 1, 2) $\Rightarrow 8-7\lambda+26+2\lambda-(29+20\lambda)=0$ $\Rightarrow 5-25\lambda=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{5}$ d.r, s of normal to P 2 $⟨\frac{33}{5},\frac{33}{5},\frac{66}{5}⟩$ or $⟨1,1,2⟩$ Angle between normals $=\frac{(\hat{i}-\frac{1}{2}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{k}).(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k})}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sqrt{6}}$ $cos\theta=\frac{1-\frac{1}{2}+1}{3}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$

questions.question_text: If two straight lines whose direction cosines are given by the relations $l+m-n=0$ , $3l^{2}+m^{2}+cnl=0$ are parallel, then the positive value of c is :
questions.question_html: If two straight lines whose direction cosines are given by the relations $l+m-n=0$ , $3l^{2}+m^{2}+cnl=0$ are parallel, then the positive value of c is :
questions.explanation_text: Given that the direction cosines satisfy $l+m-n=0$ , we find that $n=l+m$ . The other equation is $3l^{2}+m^{2}+cnl=0$ , and substituting $n=l+m$ gives $3l^{2}+m^{2}+cl(l+m)=0$ . This simplifies to $(3+c)l^{2}+clm+m^{2}=0$ . As the lines are parallel, they share the same direction ratios, so we can express $l$ in terms of $m$ , say $l=km$ . Substituting this into our equation gives $(3+c)(km)^{2}+ckm^{2}+m^{2}=0$ . This simplifies to $m^{2}[k^{2}(3+c)+kc+1]=0$ . Since $m \ne 0$ , we must have $k^{2}(3+c)+kc+1=0$ . Here, we consider the ratio $k=\frac{l}{m}$ to be constant, since the lines are parallel. The equation then becomes a quadratic equation in $k$ . As the lines are parallel, the discriminant of the quadratic equation must be equal to zero for the equation to have equal roots. Hence, the discriminant $D=(c^{2}-4(3+c))=0$ . Solving this quadratic equation gives $c^{2}-4c-12=0$ . Factoring this equation gives $(c-6)(c+2)=0$ . Solving for $c$ gives $c=6,-2$ . However, we are looking for the positive value of $c$ , so $c=6$ . Therefore, the correct answer is 6
questions.explanation_html:
Given that the direction cosines satisfy $l+m-n=0$ , we find that $n=l+m$ .

The other equation is $3l^{2}+m^{2}+cnl=0$ , and substituting $n=l+m$ gives $3l^{2}+m^{2}+cl(l+m)=0$ .

This simplifies to $(3+c)l^{2}+clm+m^{2}=0$ .

As the lines are parallel, they share the same direction ratios, so we can express $l$ in terms of $m$ , say $l=km$ . Substituting this into our equation gives $(3+c)(km)^{2}+ckm^{2}+m^{2}=0$ .

This simplifies to $m^{2}[k^{2}(3+c)+kc+1]=0$ .

Since $m \ne 0$ , we must have $k^{2}(3+c)+kc+1=0$ . Here, we consider the ratio $k=\frac{l}{m}$ to be constant, since the lines are parallel. The equation then becomes a quadratic equation in $k$ .

As the lines are parallel, the discriminant of the quadratic equation must be equal to zero for the equation to have equal roots. Hence, the discriminant $D=(c^{2}-4(3+c))=0$ .

Solving this quadratic equation gives $c^{2}-4c-12=0$ .

Factoring this equation gives $(c-6)(c+2)=0$ .

Solving for $c$ gives $c=6,-2$ .

However, we are looking for the positive value of $c$ , so $c=6$ .

Therefore, the correct answer is 6

questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{a}_{1}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $\vec{a}_{2}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ $\vec{p}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\lambda\hat{k},\vec{q}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{p} \times \vec{q}=(15-4\lambda)\hat{i}-(10-\lambda)\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ $\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ Shortest distance $=|\frac{(15-4\lambda)-2(10-\lambda)+10}{\sqrt{(15-4\lambda)^{2}+(10-\lambda)^{2}+25}}|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\Rightarrow 3(5-2\lambda)^{2}=(15-4\lambda)^{2}+(10-\lambda)^{2}+25$ $\Rightarrow 5\lambda^{2}-80\lambda+275=0$ $\therefore$ Sum of values of $\lambda=\frac{80}{5}=16$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{a}_{1}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$\vec{a}_{2}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$

$\vec{p}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\lambda\hat{k},\vec{q}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{p} \times \vec{q}=(15-4\lambda)\hat{i}-(10-\lambda)\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$

$\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ Shortest distance

$=|\frac{(15-4\lambda)-2(10-\lambda)+10}{\sqrt{(15-4\lambda)^{2}+(10-\lambda)^{2}+25}}|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\Rightarrow 3(5-2\lambda)^{2}=(15-4\lambda)^{2}+(10-\lambda)^{2}+25$

$\Rightarrow 5\lambda^{2}-80\lambda+275=0$

$\therefore$ Sum of values of $\lambda=\frac{80}{5}=16$

questions.explanation_text: $L:lx-y+3(1-l)z=1$ , $x+2y-z=2$ and plane containing the line $p:3x-8y+7z=4$ Let $\vec{n}$ be the vector parallel to L. then $\vec{n}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ l & -1 & 3(1-l) \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{aligned}|$ $=(6l-5)\hat{i}+(3-2l)\hat{j}+(2l+1)\hat{k}$ $\because$ R containing L $3(6l-5)-8(3-2l)+7(2l+1)=0$ $18l+16l+14l-15-24+7=0$ $\therefore$ $l=\frac{32}{48}=\frac{2}{3}$ Let $\theta$ be the acute angle between L and y-axis $\therefore$ $cos\theta=\frac{\frac{5}{3}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{25}{9}+\frac{49}{9}}}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{83}}$ $\therefore$ $415cos^{2}\theta=125$

questions.question_html: The foot of the perpendicular from a point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1,z=0$ to the plane $2x+3y+z=6$ lies on which one of the following curves?
questions.explanation_text: Any point on $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ , $z=0$ is $p(cos\theta,sin\theta,0)$ If foot of perpendicular of p on the plane $2x+3y+z=6$ is $(ℎ,k,l)$ then $\frac{ℎ-cos\theta}{2}=\frac{k-sin\theta}{3}=\frac{l-0}{1}$ $=-(\frac{2cos\theta+3sin\theta+0-6}{2^{2}+3^{2}+1^{2}})=r$ (let) $ℎ=2r+cos\theta,k=3r+sin\theta,l=r$ Hence, $ℎ-2l=cos\theta$ and $k-3l=sin\theta$ Hence, $(ℎ-2l)^{2}+(k-3l)^{2}=1$ When $l=6-2ℎ-3k$ Hence required locus is $(x-2(6-2x-3y))^{2}+(y-3(6-2x-3y))^{2}=1$ $\Rightarrow (5x+6y-12)^{2}+4(3x+5y-9)^{2}=1,z=6-2x-3y$

Any point on $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ , $z=0$ is $p(cos\theta,sin\theta,0)$

$\frac{ℎ-cos\theta}{2}=\frac{k-sin\theta}{3}=\frac{l-0}{1}$

$=-(\frac{2cos\theta+3sin\theta+0-6}{2^{2}+3^{2}+1^{2}})=r$ (let)

$ℎ=2r+cos\theta,k=3r+sin\theta,l=r$

Hence, $ℎ-2l=cos\theta$ and $k-3l=sin\theta$

Hence, $(ℎ-2l)^{2}+(k-3l)^{2}=1$

When $l=6-2ℎ-3k$

Hence required locus is

$(x-2(6-2x-3y))^{2}+(y-3(6-2x-3y))^{2}=1$

$\Rightarrow (5x+6y-12)^{2}+4(3x+5y-9)^{2}=1,z=6-2x-3y$

questions.question_html: A vector $\vec{a}$ is parallel to the line of intersection of the plane determined by the vectors $\hat{i},\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and the plane determined by the vectors $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ . questions.explanation_text: If $\vec{n}_{1}$ is a vector normal to the plane determined by $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ then $\vec{n}_{1}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{aligned}|=\hat{k}$ If $\vec{n}_{2}$ is a vector normal to the plane determined by $\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ then $\bar{n}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ Vector $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}$ i.e. $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ Given $\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ Cosine of acute angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}=|\frac{\vec{a}.\vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|.|\vec{b}|}|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ Obtuse angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}=\frac{3\pi}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
If $\vec{n}_{1}$ is a vector normal to the plane determined by $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ then

$\vec{n}_{1}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{aligned}|=\hat{k}$

If $\vec{n}_{2}$ is a vector normal to the plane determined by $\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ then

$\bar{n}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

Vector $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $\vec{n}_{1} \times \vec{n}_{2}$

i.e. $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$

Given $\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

Cosine of acute angle between

$\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}=|\frac{\vec{a}.\vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|.|\vec{b}|}|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Obtuse angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}=\frac{3\pi}{4}$

$\Rightarrow 12x-8y+4z+4=0$

$\Rightarrow 3x-2y+z+1=0$

And $P_{2}:2x+y+3z=0$

$\therefore$ angle between P1 and P2

$cos\theta=|\frac{6-2+3}{14}| \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$

questions.question_html: A plane passes through the points A(1, 2, 3), B(2, 3, 1) and C(2, 4, 2). If O is the origin and P is (2, $-$ 1, 1), then the projection of $\vec{OP}$ on this plane is of length :
questions.explanation_html:
A(1, 2, 3), B(2, 3, 1), C(2, 4, 2), O(0, 0, 0)

Equation of plane passing through A, B, C will be

$|\begin{aligned} x-1 & y-2 & z-3 \\ 2-1 & 3-2 & 1-3 \\ 2-1 & 4-2 & 2-3 \end{aligned}|=0$

$\Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} x-1 & y-2 & z-3 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{aligned}|=0$

$\Rightarrow (x-1)(-1+4)-(y-2)(-1+2)+(z-3)(2-1)=0$


$\Rightarrow (x-1)(3)-(y-2)(1)+(z-3)(1)=0$

$\Rightarrow 3x-3-y+2+z-3=0$

$\Rightarrow 3x-y+z-4=0$ , is the required plane.

Now, O(0, 0, 0) & P(2, $-$ 1, 1)



Plane is $3x-y+z-4=0$

O' & P' are foot of perpendiculars.

For O'

$\frac{x-0}{3}=\frac{y-0}{-1}=\frac{z-0}{1}=\frac{-(0-0+0-4)}{9+1+1}$

$\frac{x}{3}=\frac{y}{-1}=\frac{z}{1}=\frac{4}{11}$

$\Rightarrow O^{'}(\frac{12}{11},\frac{-4}{11},\frac{4}{11})$

for P'

$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{1}=\frac{-(3(2)-(-1)+1-4)}{9+1+1}$

$\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{1}=(\frac{-4}{11})$

$P^{'}(\frac{-12}{11}+2,\frac{4}{11}-1,\frac{-4}{11}+1)$

$\Rightarrow P^{'}(\frac{10}{11},\frac{-7}{11},\frac{7}{11})$

$O^{'}P^{'}=\sqrt{(\frac{10}{11}-\frac{12}{11})^{2}+(\frac{-7}{11}+\frac{4}{11})^{2}+(\frac{7}{11}-\frac{4}{11})^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow O^{'}P^{'}=\frac{1}{11}\sqrt{4+9+9}$

$\Rightarrow O^{'}P^{'}=\frac{\sqrt{22}}{11}$

$\Rightarrow O^{'}P^{'}=\frac{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{11}}{11}$

$\Rightarrow O^{'}P^{'}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{11}}$

questions.question_text: The vector equation of the plane passing through the intersection of the planes $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})=-2$ , and the point (1, 0, 2) is :
questions.question_html:
The vector equation of the plane passing through the intersection

of the planes $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})=-2$ , and the point (1, 0, 2) is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, point (1, 0, 2) Equation of plane = $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})=-2$ Equation of plane passing through the intersection of given planes is $[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]+\lambda[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$ $\because$ This plane passes through point (1, 0, 2) i.e., vector $(\hat{i}+2\hat{k})$ $\therefore$ $[(\hat{i}+2\hat{k}).(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]+\lambda[(\hat{i}+2\hat{k}).(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$ $\Rightarrow (3-1)+\lambda(1+2)=0$ $\Rightarrow 2+\lambda \times 3=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=-2/3$ Hence, equation of required plane is $[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]+(\frac{-2}{3})[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $3[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]-2[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=7$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, point (1, 0, 2)

Equation of plane =

$\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})=-2$

Equation of plane passing through the intersection of given planes is

$[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]+\lambda[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$

$\because$ This plane passes through point (1, 0, 2) i.e.,

vector $(\hat{i}+2\hat{k})$

$\therefore$ $[(\hat{i}+2\hat{k}).(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]+\lambda[(\hat{i}+2\hat{k}).(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$

$\Rightarrow (3-1)+\lambda(1+2)=0$

$\Rightarrow 2+\lambda \times 3=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=-2/3$

Hence, equation of required plane is

$[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1]+(\frac{-2}{3})[\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-2\hat{j})+2]=0$

questions.question_html:
Let $\lambda$ be an integer. If the shortest distance between the lines

x $-$ $\lambda$ = 2y $-$ 1 = $-$ 2z and x = y + 2 $\lambda$ = z $-$ $\lambda$ is $\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2\sqrt{2}}$ , then the value of | $\lambda$ | is _________.
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{x-\lambda}{1}=\frac{y-\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z}{-\frac{1}{2}}$ $\frac{x-\lambda}{2}=\frac{y-\frac{1}{2}}{1}=\frac{2}{-1}$ ....... (1) Point on line = $(\lambda,\frac{1}{2},0)$ $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+2\lambda}{1}=\frac{z-\lambda}{1}$ ....... (2) Point on line = $(0,-2\lambda,\lambda)$ Distance between skew lines $=\frac{[\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}\vec{b}_{1}\vec{b}_{2}]}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}$ $|\begin{aligned} \lambda & \frac{1}{2}+2\lambda & -\lambda \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $\bar{|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|}$ $=\frac{|-5\lambda-\frac{3}{2}|}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2\sqrt{2}}$ $=|10\lambda+3|=7 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1$ $\Rightarrow |\lambda|=1$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{x-\lambda}{1}=\frac{y-\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z}{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Point on line = $(\lambda,\frac{1}{2},0)$

$\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+2\lambda}{1}=\frac{z-\lambda}{1}$ ....... (2)

Point on line = $(0,-2\lambda,\lambda)$

Distance between skew lines $=\frac{[\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{1}\vec{b}_{1}\vec{b}_{2}]}{|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}|}$

$|\begin{aligned} \lambda & \frac{1}{2}+2\lambda & -\lambda \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$\bar{|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|}$

$=\frac{|-5\lambda-\frac{3}{2}|}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2\sqrt{2}}$

$=|10\lambda+3|=7 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1$

$\Rightarrow |\lambda|=1$

questions.question_text: The equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}.(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})+4=0$ and parallel to the x-axis is :
questions.question_html: The equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}.(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})+4=0$ and parallel to the x-axis is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of planes are $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1=0 \Rightarrow x+y+z-1=0$ and $\vec{r}.(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})+4=0 \Rightarrow 2x+3y-z+4=0$ equation of planes through line of intersection of these planes is :- $(x+y+z-1)+\lambda(2x+3y-z+4)=0$ $\Rightarrow (1+2\lambda)x+(1+3\lambda)y+(1-\lambda)z-1+4\lambda=0$ But this plane is parallel to x-axis whose direction are (1, 0, 0) $\therefore$ $(1+2\lambda)1+(1+3\lambda)0+(1-\lambda)0=0$ $\lambda=-\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ Required plane is $0x+(1-\frac{3}{2})y+(1+\frac{1}{2})z-1+4(\frac{-1}{2})=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{-y}{2}+\frac{3}{2}z-3=0$ $\Rightarrow y-3z+6=0$ $\Rightarrow \vec{r}.(\hat{j}-3\hat{k})+6=0$ Ans.
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of planes are

$\vec{r}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-1=0 \Rightarrow x+y+z-1=0$

and $\vec{r}.(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})+4=0 \Rightarrow 2x+3y-z+4=0$

equation of planes through line of intersection of these planes is :-

$(x+y+z-1)+\lambda(2x+3y-z+4)=0$

$\Rightarrow (1+2\lambda)x+(1+3\lambda)y+(1-\lambda)z-1+4\lambda=0$

But this plane is parallel to x-axis whose direction are (1, 0, 0)

$\therefore$ $(1+2\lambda)1+(1+3\lambda)0+(1-\lambda)0=0$

$\lambda=-\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$ Required plane is

$0x+(1-\frac{3}{2})y+(1+\frac{1}{2})z-1+4(\frac{-1}{2})=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{-y}{2}+\frac{3}{2}z-3=0$

$\Rightarrow y-3z+6=0$

$\Rightarrow \vec{r}.(\hat{j}-3\hat{k})+6=0$ Ans.

questions.question_html: A plane P contains the line $x+2y+3z+1=0=x-y-z-6$ , and is perpendicular to the plane $-2x+y+z+8=0$ . Then which of the following points lies on P?
questions.explanation_text: Equation of plane P can be assumed as P : x + 2y + 3z + 1 + $\lambda$ (x $-$ y $-$ z $-$ 6) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ P : (1 + $\lambda$ )x + (2 $-$ $\lambda$ )y + (3 $-$ $\lambda$ )z + 1 $-$ 6 $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow \vec{n}_{1}=(1+\lambda)\hat{i}+(2-\lambda)\hat{j}+(3-\lambda)\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{n}_{1}.\vec{n}_{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ 2(1 + $\lambda$ ) $-$ (2 $-$ $\lambda$ ) $-$ (3 $-$ $\lambda$ ) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 2 + 2 $\lambda$ $-$ 2 + $\lambda$ $-$ 3 + $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $P:\frac{7x}{4}+\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{9z}{4}-\frac{14}{4}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ 7x + 5y + 9z = 14 (0, 1, 1) lies on P.
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of plane P can be assumed as

P : x + 2y + 3z + 1 + $\lambda$ (x $-$ y $-$ z $-$ 6) = 0

$\Rightarrow$ P : (1 + $\lambda$ )x + (2 $-$ $\lambda$ )y + (3 $-$ $\lambda$ )z + 1 $-$ 6 $\lambda$ = 0

$\therefore$ $\vec{n}_{1}.\vec{n}_{2}=0$

questions.question_html: Let L be the line of intersection of planes $\vec{r}.(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=2$ and $\vec{r}.(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})=2$ . If $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the foot of perpendicular on L from the point (1, 2, 0), then the value of $35(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $P_{1}:x-y+2z=2$ $P_{2}:2x+y-3=2$ Let line of Intersection of planes P 1 and P 2 cuts xy plane in point Q. $\Rightarrow$ z-coordinate of point Q is zero $\Rightarrow \begin{aligned} x-y=2 \\ and2x+y=2 \end{aligned}} \Rightarrow x=\frac{4}{3},y=\frac{-2}{3}$ $\Rightarrow Q(\frac{4}{3},\frac{-2}{3},0)$ Vector parallel to the line of intersection $\vec{a}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}|=-\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ Equation of Line of intersection $\frac{x-\frac{4}{3}}{-1}=\frac{y+\frac{2}{3}}{5}=\frac{z-0}{3}=\lambda$ (say) Let coordinates of foot of perpendicular be $F(-\lambda+\frac{4}{3},5\lambda-\frac{2}{3},3\lambda)$ $\vec{PF}=(-\lambda+\frac{1}{3})\hat{i}+(5\lambda-\frac{8}{3})\hat{j}+(3\lambda)\hat{k}$ $\vec{PF}.\vec{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda-\frac{1}{3}+25\lambda\frac{-40}{3}+9\lambda=0$ $\Rightarrow 35\lambda=\frac{41}{3} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{41}{105}$ Now, $\alpha=-\lambda+\frac{4}{3},\beta=5\lambda-\frac{2}{3},\gamma=3\lambda$ $\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta+\gamma=7\lambda+\frac{2}{3}$ $=7(\frac{41}{105})+\frac{2}{3}$ $=\frac{51}{15}$ $\Rightarrow 35(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\frac{51}{15} \times 35=119$
questions.explanation_html:
$P_{1}:x-y+2z=2$

$P_{2}:2x+y-3=2$


Let line of Intersection of planes P1 and P2 cuts xy plane in point Q.

$\Rightarrow$ z-coordinate of point Q is zero

$\Rightarrow \begin{aligned} x-y=2 \\ and2x+y=2 \end{aligned}} \Rightarrow x=\frac{4}{3},y=\frac{-2}{3}$

$\Rightarrow Q(\frac{4}{3},\frac{-2}{3},0)$

Vector parallel to the line of intersection

$\vec{a}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}|=-\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

Equation of Line of intersection

$\frac{x-\frac{4}{3}}{-1}=\frac{y+\frac{2}{3}}{5}=\frac{z-0}{3}=\lambda$ (say)

Let coordinates of foot of perpendicular be

$F(-\lambda+\frac{4}{3},5\lambda-\frac{2}{3},3\lambda)$

$\vec{PF}=(-\lambda+\frac{1}{3})\hat{i}+(5\lambda-\frac{8}{3})\hat{j}+(3\lambda)\hat{k}$

$\vec{PF}.\vec{a}=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda-\frac{1}{3}+25\lambda\frac{-40}{3}+9\lambda=0$

$\Rightarrow 35\lambda=\frac{41}{3} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{41}{105}$

Now, $\alpha=-\lambda+\frac{4}{3},\beta=5\lambda-\frac{2}{3},\gamma=3\lambda$

$\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta+\gamma=7\lambda+\frac{2}{3}$

$=7(\frac{41}{105})+\frac{2}{3}$

$=\frac{51}{15}$

$\Rightarrow 35(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\frac{51}{15} \times 35=119$

questions.question_text: Let the position vectors of two points P and Q be 3 $\hat{i}$ $-$ $\hat{j}$ + 2 $\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}$ + 2 $\hat{j}$ $-$ 4 $\hat{k}$ , respectively. Let R and S be two points such that the direction ratios of lines PR and QS are (4, $-$ 1, 2) and ( $-$ 2, 1, $-$ 2), respectively. Let lines PR and QS intersect at T. If the vector $\vec{TA}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{PR}$ and $\vec{QS}$ and the length of vector $\vec{TA}$ is $\sqrt{5}$ units, then the modulus of a position vector of A is :
questions.question_html: Let the position vectors of two points P and Q be 3 $\hat{i}$ $-$ $\hat{j}$ + 2 $\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}$ + 2 $\hat{j}$ $-$ 4 $\hat{k}$ , respectively. Let R and S be two points such that the direction ratios of lines PR and QS are (4, $-$ 1, 2) and ( $-$ 2, 1, $-$ 2), respectively. Let lines PR and QS intersect at T. If the vector $\vec{TA}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{PR}$ and $\vec{QS}$ and the length of vector $\vec{TA}$ is $\sqrt{5}$ units, then the modulus of a position vector of A is :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{p}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ & $\vec{Q}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ $\vec{v}_{PR}=(4,-1,2)$ & $\vec{v}_{QS}=(-2,1,-2)$ $L_{PR}:\vec{r}=(3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})+\lambda(4,-1,2)$ $L_{QS}:\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k})+\mu(-2,1,-2)$ Now T on PR = $⟨3+4\lambda,-1-\lambda,2+2\lambda⟩$ Similarly T on QS = (1 $-$ 2 $\mu$ , 2 + $\mu$ , $-$ 4 $-$ 2 $\mu$ ) For $\lambda$ & $\mu$ : $\begin{aligned} 3+4\lambda=1-2\mu \Rightarrow \mu+2\lambda=-1 \\ -1-\lambda=2+\mu \Rightarrow \mu+\lambda=-3 \end{aligned}}\begin{aligned} \lambda=2 \\ \mu=-5 \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow$ T : (11, $-$ 3, 6) D.R. of TA = $\vec{v}_{QS}$ $\times$ $\vec{v}_{PR}$ = $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -1 & 2 \end{aligned}|=0\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $L_{TA}:\vec{r}=(11\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+6\hat{k})+\lambda(-4\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$ Now A = (11, $-$ 3 $-$ 4 $\lambda$ , 6 $-$ 2 $\lambda$ ) Given, TA = $\sqrt{5}$ $(-3+4\lambda+3)^{2}+(6+2\lambda-6)^{2}=5$ $16\lambda^{2}+4\lambda^{2}=5$ 20 $\lambda$ 2 = 5 $\lambda$ = $\pm$ $\frac{1}{2}$ $\begin{aligned} A:(11,-3-2,6-1) & ; & A:(11,-3+2,6+1) \\ |A|=\sqrt{121+25+25} & ; & |A|=\sqrt{121+1+49} \\ =\sqrt{171} & ; & \sqrt{171} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{p}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ & $\vec{Q}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$

$\vec{v}_{PR}=(4,-1,2)$ & $\vec{v}_{QS}=(-2,1,-2)$



$L_{PR}:\vec{r}=(3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})+\lambda(4,-1,2)$

$L_{QS}:\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k})+\mu(-2,1,-2)$

Now T on PR = $⟨3+4\lambda,-1-\lambda,2+2\lambda⟩$

Similarly T on QS = (1 $-$ 2 $\mu$ , 2 + $\mu$ , $-$ 4 $-$ 2 $\mu$ )

For $\lambda$ & $\mu$ : $\begin{aligned} 3+4\lambda=1-2\mu \Rightarrow \mu+2\lambda=-1 \\ -1-\lambda=2+\mu \Rightarrow \mu+\lambda=-3 \end{aligned}}\begin{aligned} \lambda=2 \\ \mu=-5 \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow$ T : (11, $-$ 3, 6)

D.R. of TA = $\vec{v}_{QS}$ $\times$ $\vec{v}_{PR}$

= $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -1 & 2 \end{aligned}|=0\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

$L_{TA}:\vec{r}=(11\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+6\hat{k})+\lambda(-4\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$

Now A = (11, $-$ 3 $-$ 4 $\lambda$ , 6 $-$ 2 $\lambda$ )

Given, TA = $\sqrt{5}$

$(-3+4\lambda+3)^{2}+(6+2\lambda-6)^{2}=5$

$16\lambda^{2}+4\lambda^{2}=5$

20 $\lambda$ 2 = 5

$\lambda$ = $\pm$ $\frac{1}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} A:(11,-3-2,6-1) & ; & A:(11,-3+2,6+1) \\ |A|=\sqrt{121+25+25} & ; & |A|=\sqrt{121+1+49} \\ =\sqrt{171} & ; & \sqrt{171} \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow 20+2m^{2}=7m^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $m^{2}=4 \Rightarrow |m|=2$

questions.question_text: If the shortest distance between the straight lines $3(x-1)=6(y-2)=2(z-1)$ and $4(x-2)=2(y-\lambda)=(z-3),\lambda \in R$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{38}}$ , then the integral value of $\lambda$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If the shortest distance between the straight lines $3(x-1)=6(y-2)=2(z-1)$ and $4(x-2)=2(y-\lambda)=(z-3),\lambda \in R$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{38}}$ , then the integral value of $\lambda$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $L_{1}:\frac{(x-1)}{2}=\frac{(y-2)}{1}=\frac{(z-1)}{3}\vec{r_{1}}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $L_{2}:\frac{(x-2)}{1}=\frac{y-\lambda}{2}=\frac{z-3}{4}\vec{r_{2}}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ Shortest distance = Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}$ $=\frac{|\vec{a}.(\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}})|}{|\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}|}$ $|\vec{a}.(\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}})|=|\begin{aligned} 1 & \lambda-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{aligned}|=|14-5\lambda|$ $|\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}|=\sqrt{38}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{38}}=\frac{|14-5\lambda|}{\sqrt{38}}$ $\Rightarrow |14-5\lambda|=1$ $\Rightarrow 14-5\lambda=1$ or $14-5\lambda=-1$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{13}{5}$ or 3 $\therefore$ Integral value of $\lambda$ = 3.
questions.explanation_html:
$L_{1}:\frac{(x-1)}{2}=\frac{(y-2)}{1}=\frac{(z-1)}{3}\vec{r_{1}}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$L_{2}:\frac{(x-2)}{1}=\frac{y-\lambda}{2}=\frac{z-3}{4}\vec{r_{2}}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$


Shortest distance = Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}$

$=\frac{|\vec{a}.(\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}})|}{|\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}|}$

$|\vec{a}.(\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}})|=|\begin{aligned} 1 & \lambda-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{aligned}|=|14-5\lambda|$

$|\vec{r_{1}} \times \vec{r_{2}}|=\sqrt{38}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{38}}=\frac{|14-5\lambda|}{\sqrt{38}}$

$\Rightarrow |14-5\lambda|=1$

$\Rightarrow 14-5\lambda=1$ or $14-5\lambda=-1$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{13}{5}$ or 3

$\therefore$ Integral value of $\lambda$ = 3.
